findings.claim: Teilupdates überschreiben ausgelassene Einstellungen mit Defaults, wenn das vorherige Lesen fehlschlägt.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein Kanal hat approval_mode=full_auto, timezone=America/New_York und subtitles_enabled=false. Beim PUT mit ausschließlich {"timezone":"Europe/London"} gelingt die Kanalauflösung, aber die folgende Einstellungsabfrage verliert ihre Verbindung. Bis zum anschließenden Schreiben ist die Datenbank wieder erreichbar. Der Handler speichert nun zusätzlich approval_mode=manual und subtitles_enabled=true und meldet Erfolg. Derselbe Fehler tritt beim Plattform-Teilupdate auf: Ein fehlgeschlagenes Bestandslesen setzt ausgelassene Kadenzwerte und auto_post auf Defaults. Beim VOD-Toggle ohne privacy wird eine vorhandene Sichtbarkeit unlisted durch private ersetzt.
findings.evidence: Feste Basis 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/posting_plan.rs:237-254 wandelt SQL-Fehler mittels .ok().flatten() in StreamerSettings::default() um. Die Handlerstelle verwendet diesen Ersatz für ausgelassene Felder und schreibt den vollständigen Datensatz bei Zeilen 3271-3320; save_streamer_settings überschreibt alle drei Werte bei posting_plan.rs:266-284. Geprüfte Zwillinge: load_platform_schedules bei posting_plan.rs:288-318 und Plattform-Handler bei social_media.rs:3380-3462; get_vod_archive_settings bei /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/vod_archive.rs:55-89 und VOD-Handler bei social_media.rs:3629-3652. Die Speicherung erfolgt jeweils getrennt vom fehlgeschlagenen Lesen.
findings.expected_behavior: Ein Teilupdate muss ausgelassene Werte erhalten oder bei fehlgeschlagenem Bestandslesen mit Serverfehler abbrechen. Das Soll ist durch die current-Fallbacks im Handler und ausdrücklich durch social_media.rs:3629-3636 sowie den Test social_media.rs:6229-6239 belegt: Ein Toggle ohne privacy erhält die bisherige Sichtbarkeit. Defaults sind laut posting_plan.rs:236 und vod_archive.rs:48-49 für fehlende Datensätze vorgesehen, nicht als zuverlässiger Ersatz für vorhandene, gerade nicht lesbare Werte.
findings.countermeasures: required_streamer_scope prüft Existenz und Identität vorab; Schreibfehler werden als HTTP 500 beantwortet. Beides verhindert keinen einzelnen späteren Lesefehler mit erfolgreicher Folgespeicherung. Es gibt weder eine gemeinsame Transaktion noch eine Fehlerkennzeichnung im Rückgabewert der Loader. Statische Prüfung, keine Tests oder Datenbankzugriffe ausgeführt.

findings.claim: Enrichment-GET meldet erfolgreiche fiktive Metadaten, wenn die Enrichment-Persistenz nicht erreichbar ist.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein vorhandener Clip ist für den Aufrufer lesbar. Die Enrichment-Tabelle ist nicht verfügbar, beispielsweise fehlt sie in einer unvollständigen Datenbankinstallation, während Clip- und Hashtag-Tabellen funktionieren. Beide Enrichment-Leseversuche und der INSERT schlagen fehl. GET /social-media/api/admin/clips/{id}/enrichment antwortet trotzdem mit HTTP 200, status=pending, leeren Hashtags und null-Titeln, obwohl keine entsprechende Zeile angelegt oder gelesen wurde.
findings.evidence: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/enrichment.rs:121-136 ersetzt Leseprobleme durch None. ensure_enrichment_row bei Zeilen 140-193 protokolliert einen fehlgeschlagenen INSERT, liest erneut und erzeugt anschließend einen synthetischen EnrichmentRecord. Die Primärstelle /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/social_media.rs:2702-2706 serialisiert diesen Datensatz ohne Fehlerprüfung. clip_metadata_json bei Zeilen 2446-2463 prüft lediglich einen nachfolgenden Clip-Identitätszugriff, nicht die Enrichment-Persistenz. Die Route ist bei /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:412-415 registriert.
findings.expected_behavior: Der Endpoint muss einen Speicherfehler anzeigen, statt einen nicht existierenden oder nicht gelesenen Datensatz als erfolgreichen Zustand auszugeben. Der Test social_media.rs:6382-6393 beschreibt pending als Ergebnis einer tatsächlich angelegten Zeile. Enrichment-PUT meldet entsprechende Speicherprobleme bereits als save_failed bei social_media.rs:2628-2633 und 2674-2678.
findings.countermeasures: Auth, Ownership, Clip-Existenz und int4-Konvertierung werden vorher geprüft. Sie betreffen die Clip-Tabelle und verhindern den separaten Fehler der Enrichment-Tabelle nicht. Warnungen im Serverprotokoll existieren, aber der Client erhält keine Fehlermeldung. Keine Laufzeitprobe ausgeführt.

findings.claim: Report- und Clip-Analytics-GET melden Datenbankfehler als erfolgreiche leere Listen.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein Admin ruft die Report-Liste ohne Streamerfilter auf. Die SQL-Abfrage auf social_media_reports schlägt fehl, etwa wegen einer fehlenden Tabelle oder eines Verbindungsfehlers. Statt eines Serverfehlers kommt HTTP 200 mit {"items":[]}. Beim geprüften Zwilling funktionieren Auth und die Clip-Abfrage, aber die separate Analytics-Abfrage schlägt fehl; auch dort erscheint ein Clip mit angeblich keinen Analytics-Snapshots statt einer Fehlermeldung.
findings.evidence: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/analytics.rs:274-292 verwirft list_reports-Fehler mit .unwrap_or_default(). Der Primärhandler bei /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/social_media.rs:2886-2896 gibt diese Liste bedingungslos als JSON-Erfolg aus. Zwilling: list_clip_analytics bei analytics.rs:189-207 mit demselben Fehlerverlust und clip_analytics_get_handler bei social_media.rs:2761-2766. Beide Routen sind bei /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:428-435 registriert.
findings.expected_behavior: Eine leere Ergebnisliste darf nur eine erfolgreich gelesene leere Datenmenge darstellen. Fehlgeschlagene Lesezugriffe müssen als Serverfehler erkennbar bleiben. Die benachbarte Clip-Abfrage unterscheidet Fehler bereits ausdrücklich von fehlenden Daten bei social_media.rs:2184-2189. Der vorhandene Test /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/social_media_status_tests.rs:76-111 verlangt für denselben Dashboard-Bereich ausdrücklich HTTP 500 statt eines vorgetäuschten fehlenden Zustands.
findings.countermeasures: Reports sind Admin-only; Analytics erfordert zusätzlich Scope und Clip-Existenz. Beim ungefilterten Admin-Reportaufruf findet keine vorherige Datenbankabfrage statt, die den Fehler abfangen könnte. Beim Analytics-Zwilling schützt die erfolgreich gelesene Clip-Tabelle nicht vor Fehlern der separaten Analytics-Tabelle. Keine Tests oder Datenbankprobes ausgeführt.

findings.claim: Approval- und Preview-GET behandeln fehlgeschlagene Zustandsabfragen wie fehlenden Zustand.

findings.claim: Preview Range requests buffer the entire MP4 before selecting and copying the requested range.
findings.failure_scenario: An authorized owner or admin opens concurrent slow downloads of a ready preview using Range: bytes=0-. For file size S and N unfinished responses, the bodies retain at least N*S bytes, with additional full-file allocations during response construction. For example, 64 responses holding a 32 MiB preview retain 2 GiB before process overhead. If available memory is below that amount, the dashboard can fail allocation or be OOM-killed. Even bytes=0-0 requires reading the whole file. This is a static failure condition, not a production reproduction.
findings.evidence: At fixed SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, lines 4080-4087 read the complete preview with tokio::fs::read before processing Range. Lines 4124-4135 copy the selected range into another Vec and retain it in Body. The route is registered at /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:425-426. Reviewed router layers add authentication-related guards, tracing, compression and security headers, but no concurrency or response-buffer limit. The targeted helper lookup found only this caller.
findings.expected_behavior: Preserve the existing 200/206 response semantics without requiring a complete video allocation for each range request. A bounded file stream or an explicit transfer resource budget would prevent this amplification. Classified C because the required deployment memory/concurrency budget is unspecified and production ingress protection was not verified.
findings.countermeasures: The handler requires an admin or a granted partner owning the clip through preview_scope_and_child. Preview generation limits duration to 60 seconds, and encoding limits frame rate, reducing typical file sizes. Neither is a byte-size or concurrent-response memory ceiling. No unauthenticated exploit is asserted. Installed proxy settings and actual memory limits were deliberately not probed.

findings.claim: Social-media OAuth permits linking a victim's provider account to an attacker's Twitch account.
findings.failure_scenario: With YouTube OAuth configured, a Social-Media-enabled malicious partner starts the flow for their own Twitch account and forwards the returned Google authorization URL, including its valid state and PKCE challenge, to a victim. If the victim authorizes the legitimate application within ten minutes, the callback succeeds from the victim's browser without any initiating-session or browser check. The victim's YouTube credentials are stored under the attacker's Twitch ID. Uploading the attacker's own clips then uses the victim's YouTube account. This requires victim consent to the application, but not consent to giving the attacker control.
findings.evidence: Static review at SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. oauth_callback_handler(3770-3805) accepts pool, path and query only, with no session or browser nonce. OAuthManager::generate_auth_url(131-178) stores state with channel ID, platform, redirect and verifier, but no browser/session binding. consume_state_token(222-262) checks expiration, single use, platform and redirect only. handle_callback(192-211) persists provider credentials under the state-derived Twitch ID; save_encrypted_tokens(697-730) binds that ID into the credential row. The public router explicitly registers callback aliases at lib.rs:201-220. UploadWorker::resolve_upload(792-815) selects credentials using the clip owner's Twitch ID, establishing the posting impact. No tests or runtime probes were executed.
findings.expected_behavior: A provider-account linking callback must be bound to the browser/session that initiated the linking transaction, before exchanging or saving credentials. Local ownership checks already restrict a partner's actions to the session-derived Twitch ID; transferring an authorization URL must not let that partner acquire another browser user's provider account.
findings.countermeasures: Existing protections include authenticated and granted access at OAuth start, server-derived Twitch scope, random hashed state, a ten-minute expiry, atomic single-use consumption, platform/redirect matching, PKCE for YouTube/TikTok and encrypted credential storage. They all pass for an unchanged authorization URL transferred to another browser. The CSRF middleware checks write methods only; the callback is a public GET. Both callback aliases use the same handler, and supported providers share this missing browser binding. Bind each OAuth transaction to an initiating-session or dedicated browser nonce and validate it before state consumption and token exchange. Deployed reverse-proxy configuration was not probed.

findings.claim: A quota-booking failure during manual upload deletes the file but leaves its committed clip record, preventing retry with the same clip ID.
findings.failure_scenario: Upload a valid MP4 with clip_id=good1 for an existing authorized streamer. The clip INSERT succeeds, but the subsequent quota UPDATE fails, for example because the database connection becomes unavailable. The endpoint returns 500 and removes good1.mp4. The committed pending clip still references that deleted file. Retrying good1 returns 409 because the existing database record is detected.
findings.evidence: All source inspected at 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. register_manual_upload executes its INSERT directly on PgPool at clip_manager.rs:66-82, then propagates mark_kontingent_verbrauch failure with '?' at 89-91. The quota helper performs a separate UPDATE at clip/repository.rs:157-166. process_uploaded_clip removes final_path for every ManualUploadError::Db at social_media.rs:931-937 but performs no database rollback or row deletion. The retry check is clip_manager.rs:40-48.
findings.expected_behavior: A failed registration must not retain a clip record pointing to a file its own error cleanup deleted. The upload success test at social_media.rs:7094-7122 establishes that a registered clip has its saved MP4 and that an existing registration blocks reuse of its ID.
findings.countermeasures: Target identity, streamer existence, MIME, duration and duplicate checks run before registration, but do not protect against failure after the INSERT. Layout application is explicitly best-effort; quota booking is not, because its error propagates. No transaction encloses insertion and quota booking.

findings.claim: Clip-layout PUT reports successful set or clear operations even when the database write fails.
findings.failure_scenario: An authorized user changes an existing clip's layout while SELECT succeeds but UPDATE fails, for example due to a statement timeout on a locked row. The endpoint returns 200 containing the requested layout_override although the old override remains stored. Sending layout=null under the same condition similarly claims the override was cleared when it was not.
findings.evidence: Both branches discard the Result from set_clip_layout_override using 'let _ =' at social_media.rs:1140 and 1153. layout.rs:546-561 returns the UPDATE error through '?'. The response uses null or the requested layout rather than a confirmed stored override. The frontend fetchJson accepts every 2xx response at socialMedia.ts:90-108; setClipLayoutOverride uses it at 257-265.
findings.expected_behavior: The PUT must report failure when persisting or clearing the override fails. The set-and-clear test at social_media.rs:5137-5185 establishes the two intended effects. The adjacent streamer-layout PUT already returns 500 on write failure at 1086-1092.
findings.countermeasures: Authentication, partner scope, clip existence, access and layout validation are present. They do not inspect the write result. The later effective-layout read can return the old layout or a fallback but cannot turn the failed UPDATE into a successful mutation.

findings.claim: Multipart parsing errors can be ignored after a complete file part, allowing a malformed upload request to return 201.
findings.failure_scenario: An authorized partner sends a complete valid MP4 file part followed by a malformed multipart part header. next_field returns an error after bytes has been populated. The loop exits as if the body ended normally, and the handler registers the file and returns 201 despite the malformed request. Errors reading later title or clip_id fields can likewise silently drop supplied metadata.
findings.evidence: The loop is 'while let Ok(Some(field)) = multipart.next_field().await' at 955, so Err and normal end both leave the loop without an error response. Field bytes/text errors are converted to None with '.ok()' at 957-960. Only the presence of previously collected bytes is checked at 964. Registration then proceeds at 993-1005.
findings.expected_behavior: A multipart parsing or field-read failure must reject the request rather than commit the successfully parsed prefix as a complete upload. Body-size failures should retain their rejection status instead of becoming missing fields or successful prefix processing.
findings.countermeasures: The upload route has a 201 MiB body limit at lib.rs:307-312; process_uploaded_clip validates the collected file's size, MIME and duration. Those checks validate only the retained file bytes, not successful parsing of the entire multipart request. Partner identity and CSRF protections restrict callers but do not handle parser errors.

findings.claim: Batch upload reports success with zero errors when fetching the streamer's pending clips fails.
findings.failure_scenario: An administrator submits twitch_user_id=42, platforms=[youtube], apply_default_template=false for an existing streamer with pending clips. Resolving the streamer succeeds, but the pending-clips SELECT fails, for example because of a database statement timeout. Nothing is queued, yet the response is 200 with success=true and stats={queued:0,skipped:0,errors:0}.
findings.evidence: batch_upload_all_new initializes all statistics to zero at clip_manager.rs:222-226 and replaces the failed pending-clips fetch with an empty vector at 255-262. Only queue_upload failures increment errors at 291-305. The handler unconditionally emits success=true at social_media.rs:1552-1557.
findings.expected_behavior: Failure to read the clips to be queued must be surfaced as an operation failure or nonzero error result, not as an error-free empty batch. The endpoint promises to enqueue all new clips, and its test at 7128-7158 verifies that an eligible clip produces a queued item.
findings.countermeasures: Scope, platform presence, plan and target-existence checks run first. None protects against a later clips-query failure. Per-clip queue errors are counted, but the initial query error is discarded before that loop can run.

findings.claim: Mark-uploaded returns success for a nonexistent clip when an administrator omits the streamer scope.
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated administrator posts clip_id=99999 and platforms=[youtube], with no twitch_user_id, when that clip does not exist. The endpoint returns 200 with success=true and 'Clip marked as uploaded', although no row was changed.
findings.evidence: resolve_sm_scope returns None for an administrator without a requested scope at social_media.rs:525-529. The ownership check at 1611-1621 is skipped for that scope, and there is no existence check. mark_clip_uploaded executes UPDATE statements without examining rows_affected at clip_manager.rs:163-174, commits, and returns true at 187. The subsequent publication-status updates also do not check affected rows.
findings.expected_behavior: A successful mark operation must concern an existing clip and change or confirm its upload marker. The test at social_media.rs:6830-6850 checks the stored flag after success. Missing clips must not receive a fabricated mutation-success response.
findings.countermeasures: Positive clip-ID and nonempty-platform validation exist. A partner or scoped administrator is constrained by ownership checks, so the demonstrated path is specifically the authorized unscoped administrator path. A database constraint cannot make an UPDATE matching zero rows fail.

findings.claim: Pagination offset multiplication overflows for accepted page numbers in both vocabulary and clip listing.
findings.failure_scenario: Request page=9223372036854775807&page_size=2 as an administrator. Both values pass parsing and clamping. In the release profile, (page-1)*page_size wraps to -4. The vocabulary helper clamps that offset to zero and returns first-page entries labeled with the huge page number. The clip-list query sends OFFSET -4 to PostgreSQL and returns 500. With overflow checks enabled, the same input panics instead.
findings.evidence: Unchecked i64 multiplication occurs at social_media.rs:1693 and the twin at 2304. The preceding parsers accept any positive i64 page. list_vocab clamps offset.max(0) at vocab.rs:141-142, while admin_clips_handler binds the wrapped offset directly at social_media.rs:2323-2324. Cargo.toml:128-130 defines no release overflow-check override.
findings.expected_behavior: Pagination must not wrap into another page, generate a negative database OFFSET, or panic on a syntactically accepted external input. Unrepresentable offsets should use the existing invalid_pagination rejection path. The vocabulary test at social_media.rs:5238-5250 establishes 400 for invalid pagination.
findings.countermeasures: page_size is bounded and page is clamped to at least one, but page has no upper bound and multiplication is unchecked. Query parameterization prevents injection, not arithmetic overflow. Both twins were read.

findings.claim: Vocabulary listing can return entries with total=0 after a count-query failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The vocabulary contains matching entries. Its COUNT query fails transiently, but the subsequent page SELECT succeeds. The endpoint returns 200 with a nonempty items list and total=0. Pagination therefore reports an empty collection even while returning its entries.
findings.evidence: list_vocab replaces a failed count with zero at vocab.rs:145-162, independently runs the row query at 164-187, and returns the combined tuple at 188. vocab_list_handler serializes that tuple without error information at social_media.rs:1694-1697. The existing test at 5223-5237 expects total=1 alongside the stored entry.
findings.expected_behavior: The total must describe the same successfully queried collection as the returned entries. A failed count must not be represented as a confirmed zero count.
findings.countermeasures: The endpoint requires administrator access and validates pagination. Neither addresses independent query failures. The API caller fetchVocab uses fetchJson, which treats this 200 response as successful data. No error marker identifies the fabricated total.

findings.claim: Vocabulary mutation handlers misreport database failures as invalid user input.
findings.failure_scenario: An administrator submits a valid vocabulary entry, or deletes a valid nonempty term, while the database is unavailable. Instead of identifying the server-side failure, the handlers return 400 with invalid_vocab or invalid_term, falsely asking the caller to correct already valid input.
findings.evidence: VocabError explicitly distinguishes validation variants from Db(sqlx::Error) at vocab.rs:16-26. Both upsert and delete propagate database errors at 227-242 and 283-287. Their handlers map every Err to BAD_REQUEST at social_media.rs:1745-1749 and 1777-1781, including Db.
findings.expected_behavior: Validation failures should remain 400; database failures must be identified as server-side failures rather than invalid vocabulary or invalid terms. This distinction already exists in the helper's error enum and in neighboring mutation handlers that use 500 for database write failure.
findings.countermeasures: Administrator authentication and input validation limit reachability and correctly reject malformed values. They do not prevent outages after valid input reaches SQL. The DB error text is included, but neither handler preserves its error category in the status or error code.

findings.claim: Discarding an existing clip can return clip_not_found when the database update fails.
findings.failure_scenario: An authorized administrator discards an existing clip while its UPDATE fails, for example due to a statement timeout. The clip remains present and undiscarded, but the endpoint returns 404 clip_not_found instead of reporting the failed write.
findings.evidence: mark_clip_discarded converts the UPDATE error to None using '.ok().flatten()' at retention.rs:139-149 and returns false. admin_clip_discard_handler interprets every false as missing clip at social_media.rs:2398-2399. No database error is propagated or logged by this helper.
findings.expected_behavior: A genuine missing clip may return 404. Failure to discard a present clip must surface as a server-side write failure, not false evidence that the clip does not exist. The handler already distinguishes read errors from missing records through clip_load_failed elsewhere.
findings.countermeasures: Authentication, positive ID, scope and partner-access guards precede the write. The unscoped administrator path passes them without checking database existence. Even a prior successful ownership query would not prevent a later UPDATE failure.

findings.claim: Streamer-layout GET reports a default layout when loading an existing saved layout fails.
findings.failure_scenario: The streamer lookup succeeds and a custom saved layout exists, but reading social_media_streamer_layout fails. GET returns 200 with a global default, is_default=true and no saved-update metadata. A user can mistake the existing custom layout for an unsaved default and overwrite it.
findings.evidence: get_streamer_layout converts SQL failure to None at layout.rs:408-417. The handler substitutes default_streamer_layout at social_media.rs:1029-1030 and sets is_default from stored.is_none() at 1050. No field distinguishes a failed read from confirmed absence.
findings.expected_behavior: If the response represents persisted state, failed reads should not claim that no saved layout exists. Classified C because the shared layout helper deliberately provides fallback-compatible Option results and no explicit HTTP failure-versus-fallback policy was found.
findings.countermeasures: required_streamer_scope proves the target exists, but queries a different table. The layout helper's fallback supports other consumers, including rendering. Changing that shared fallback policy without clarifying the endpoint contract could change intentional degraded operation.

findings.claim: Several social-media read endpoints expose database failures as successful empty data.
findings.failure_scenario: An administrator reads clips, streamer templates, last hashtags or analytics while the corresponding SQL queries fail, despite existing saved data. The endpoints return 200 with empty collections or empty summary objects, indistinguishable from a successfully queried empty account.
findings.evidence: clips_handler serializes get_clips_for_dashboard directly at 215-216; that helper logs a warning and returns Vec::new on failure at clip_manager.rs:127-135. templates_streamer_handler serializes get_streamer_templates at 358-360, whose query uses unwrap_or_default at clip_templates.rs:152-161. last_hashtags_handler at 229-230 relies on a query using .ok().flatten() at clip_templates.rs:278-287. stats_handler at 198 relies on .ok()/unwrap_or_default fallbacks in clip_analytics.rs:15-67.
findings.expected_behavior: Callers should be able to distinguish unavailable data from confirmed empty data when that distinction matters to the dashboard. Classified C because these helpers intentionally expose fallback-only return types and an explicit degraded-read policy is not documented in the inspected context.
findings.countermeasures: Unauthenticated users are rejected and partner access fails closed; an authenticated administrator still reaches these queries. Some helper failures are logged, but logs are not conveyed in the successful HTTP response. The explicitly best-effort upload-queue supplement at social_media.rs:1992-1997 was inspected and is not included in this finding.

findings.claim: Implicit TikTok approval skips mandatory posting-option validation and persistence.
findings.failure_scenario: An authorized channel has TikTok auto_post enabled with positive cadence, complete TikTok credentials, and an owned clip with no saved tiktok_post_options. POST approval decision with {"decision":"approve","platforms":[]} returns successful TikTok approval and queues the clip without posting options. At its scheduled time, the worker marks the upload failed because those options are mandatory. Supplying valid tiktok_options with the same implicit platform selection also fails because the handler never saves them.
findings.evidence: All source read at 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. The handler only calls save_choice when the request's normalized platforms explicitly contains tiktok (social_media.rs:2994-3012). findings.claim: Ein Fehler bei der Kontingentbuchung löscht die Videodatei eines bereits dauerhaft registrierten Uploads.

Der Datenbankeintrag bleibt pending und verweist auf die entfernte Datei. Die Anfrage liefert 500; ein erneuter Versuch mit derselben Clip-ID trifft auf AlreadyExists und kann den beschädigten Eintrag nicht reparieren.

findings.claim: Concurrent manual uploads with the same clip ID can delete a successfully registered video.
findings.failure_scenario: Two uploads for the same channel and clip ID both pass the final-path existence check. Request A finishes registration. Request B, which passed the check earlier, then writes and validates its temporary file, renames it over A's final file, and receives AlreadyExists from registration. B removes the final file, leaving A's successful database record without its video.
findings.evidence: Handler lines 825-843 use a shared final path and temporary path with a non-atomic exists check. Lines 901-916 rename before registering and delete the final path on AlreadyExists. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/clip_manager.rs:40-48 detects A's committed record only after B has replaced its file. The assigned upload test at handler lines 7094-7122 checks a sequential duplicate, not this interleaving.
findings.expected_behavior: A duplicate upload must return conflict without damaging the earlier successful upload, as demonstrated by the duplicate handling and assigned validation test.
findings.countermeasures: The clip_id UNIQUE constraint protects database identity, not filesystem ownership. Scope checks and upload validation do not lock the shared paths; Linux rename can replace the destination.

findings.claim: A quota-accounting failure deletes the video belonging to an already committed manual-upload record.
findings.failure_scenario: A valid manual upload is inserted successfully. The following quota-accounting UPDATE fails, for example because its database connection is interrupted. Registration returns a database error, and the handler deletes the video. The committed clip record remains and rejects retries with the same clip ID.
findings.evidence: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/clip_manager.rs:66-91 inserts using PgPool and then separately awaits mark_kontingent_verbrauch with error propagation. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/clip/repository.rs:157-165 executes the accounting UPDATE separately. Handler lines 931-937 remove the final video for that error without rolling back the inserted record.
findings.expected_behavior: Registration must not leave a persistent manual-upload record referencing a deleted video when a subsequent registration step fails. The successful path stores the video and returns its clip_db_id together.
findings.countermeasures: The unique clip ID prevents duplicate rows but makes retrying this orphaned record fail. Default-layout failures are deliberately tolerated, whereas quota-accounting errors propagate after the insert has committed.

findings.claim: Concurrent partial posting-plan updates overwrite settings omitted from the request.
findings.failure_scenario: A channel currently uses full_auto. Request A changes approval_mode to manual while request B changes only timezone. Both read the old settings. A saves manual, then B saves its merged stale record containing full_auto, undoing A's safety change even though B never requested an approval-mode change. The platform endpoint has the same race between disabling auto_post and editing posting times.

The twin handler at lines 3380-3454 performs the same read/merge/write for platform settings; the corresponding persistence helper at lines 322-352 overwrites every field.
findings.expected_behavior: Fields omitted from a partial settings request must remain unchanged. The handler explicitly falls back to current values, and assigned tests at lines 6034-6042 and 6059-6079 submit partial settings updates.
findings.countermeasures: Per-channel identity checks and unique settings keys prevent cross-channel writes and duplicate rows, but neither provides row locking across the read/write sequence or detects stale versions. HTTP middleware does not serialize these writes.

After the privacy request commits, the toggle writes its stale unlisted value back. A later enable-only toggle retains unlisted rather than the privacy setting the user saved.

The assigned test at handler lines 6229-6239 establishes that toggling without privacy must preserve it, but exercises only sequential requests.

findings.claim: A stalled ffprobe keeps a clip upload and its video buffer alive indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario: An authorized user uploads an MP4 that passes the ftyp check. The spawned ffprobe process stalls without exiting, for example while blocked on filesystem I/O. The handler remains inside get_video_info indefinitely, retaining the upload buffer of up to 200 MiB and the staged file. Concurrent affected uploads accumulate retained memory and subprocesses.

Lines 866-875 directly await get_video_info; duration validation and cleanup occur only after it returns. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/video_processor.rs:385-399 calls Command::output().await without a timeout or kill_on_drop. The inspected router and server do not install a request deadline. No runtime reproduction was performed.
findings.expected_behavior: External media validation must return a result or terminate with an upload error within a finite execution bound. The 300-second media-duration restriction must not be mistaken for an execution deadline.
findings.countermeasures: Authentication, partner access and target ownership checks restrict callers. The route caps request bodies at 201 MiB and validation caps file size at 200 MiB. These constrain input size, not subprocess runtime. Explicit validation-error cleanup cannot run while the probe is stalled. Deployment proxy behavior was not probed.

findings.claim: Repeated form selections permit thousands of sequential upstream retries in one upload request.
findings.failure_scenario: With form submission enabled, an authorized caller submits an owned clip with platforms=[] and 1,000 copies of deadlock_high in forms. The form endpoint repeatedly reaches its 30-second timeout. Each failure marks the submission failed, allowing the next duplicate to reserve and retry it. One small request therefore performs 1,000 external attempts and can remain pending for approximately 8.3 hours, rather than submitting once to the selected destination.
findings.evidence: At fixed SHA 0ecae137, forms is an unrestricted Vec<FormKey> at 1178-1179 and is processed serially without deduplication at 1355-1374. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/forms.rs:13-17 defines only three destinations; 120-126 provides a 30-second per-attempt timeout; 185-194 immediately reopens failed reservations; 323-346 records failures. The platforms loops at 1335 and 1525-1552 similarly preserve duplicate destinations, although platform queue rows are deduplicated downstream. The sibling approval normalization deduplicates its platform selections at 2910-2926.

The 30-second timeout limits each attempt, not the cumulative request duration; failed reservations specifically bypass duplicate suppression.

The same duration() path is used by save_choice(). This is a conditional subprocess-failure scenario, not a demonstrated media-triggered exploit.

In /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/video_processor.rs:385-399, get_video_info() directly awaits Command::output(), with neither a timeout nor kill_on_drop(true). The inspected route and outer middleware contain no request deadline. The sibling render cancellation test at video_processor.rs:834-845 explicitly expects its own child to be terminated and reaped after cancellation.

No runtime probe or deployment verification was performed.

The worker then rejects the old approval as an account mismatch and marks the job failed instead of uploading.

The OAuth callback does not update their approval. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-social-media/src/upload_worker.rs:967-1009 reads the queue snapshot and rejects mismatched credentials; lines 1048-1052, 661-663 and 1119-1123 make this validation error a failed job.
findings.expected_behavior: A successfully renewed approval must update the existing not-yet-started job that the enqueue operation reuses, including jobs awaiting reconnection.
findings.countermeasures: Live credential, creator-option and video-digest validation all run before saving. Parent-row locking and the active-upload guard prevent changes to begun uploads, but waiting_connection is allowed and then skipped by the update. The worker correctly blocks the stale identity; that safeguard exposes the failed recovery rather than repairing it. A fresh INSERT receives the new snapshot, but reuse does not.

blockers: The pinned bot repository does not establish the relay's generation-aware repeated DELETE semantics; the C finding remains protocol-dependent.

findings.claim: Stream-key generation-check failures are reported as a missing platform connection.
findings.failure_scenario: A connected Twitch account successfully supplies its token and stream key, but the subsequent database generation lookup times out or loses its connection. Err is treated like Ok(false), so the endpoint returns HTTP 409 and tells the streamer to connect first although their connection still exists.
findings.evidence: uplink.rs:1439-1449 accepts only Ok(true) and maps every other outcome to KeineVerbindung; streamkey_antwort at 1677-1680 translates that into the missing-connection response. target_generation.rs:43 and 57-64 propagate database/time-limit errors. The twin platform stream-key path in plattform_connect.rs:564-574 has the same defect. In contrast, platform_token.rs:426-435 explicitly maps an error from the same check to NichtLieferbar and reserves KeineVerbindung for a successful negative result.
findings.expected_behavior: Keep the generation guard fail-closed, but classify a failed lookup as a temporary operation failure rather than an absent connection. StreamKeyStand::Fehlgeschlagen already provides the retryable HTTP 502 response at uplink.rs:1685-1688.
findings.countermeasures: Session identity, CSRF, and the generation check prevent unauthorized or superseded writes. They do not correct the error classification. Earlier token-read failures are correctly distinguished at uplink.rs:1421-1427, so this loss occurs specifically at the final generation guard.

findings.claim: Disconnect cannot finish when a matching-generation DELETE reports an already-absent target.
findings.failure_scenario: The relay deletes the target, but local disconnect completion fails transiently. On retry, begin_disconnect reuses the pending generation. If the relay acknowledges that same generation with deleted:false because the target is already absent, HttpRelayZiele returns Ok(false), trennen returns RelayFehler, and local completion is never attempted. Subsequent identical replies leave the connection permanently pending while the response keeps instructing the user to retry.
findings.evidence: RelayZiele documents false as 'there was no target' at uplink.rs:1228. HttpRelayZiele:1311-1317 returns that flag after checking the generation. trennen:1507-1512 requires Ok(true), preventing finish_uplink_disconnect at 1513-1521. target_generation.rs:110-114 deliberately preserves the generation while disconnect_pending is true. The Kick/YouTube twin at plattform_connect.rs:719-730 uses the same condition.
findings.expected_behavior: A confirmed, generation-fenced absence should permit idempotent local completion without requiring another actual deletion. Obsolete or unconfirmed generations must remain rejected. Whether deleted:false constitutes such confirmation needs an explicit relay protocol agreement before changing this condition.
findings.countermeasures: Matching-generation validation and the local completion CAS protect newer connections. The FencedRelay test double in plattform_connect.rs:1501-1507 always returns true, including when no target was present, so it does not establish the real repeated-delete contract. This uncertainty makes the finding C rather than an automatic fix.

findings.claim: A mismatched PostgreSQL notification routes an event to the wrong channel.
findings.failure_scenario: An open socket belongs to channel A. Row 700 belongs to channel B and has not been delivered or excluded by A's delivery cursor. A database sender publishes {"channel_id":"A","id":700} on obs_dock. The listener fetches B's payload using only id=700 and broadcasts it to A. Exploitation requires permission to publish a mismatched PostgreSQL notification; an untrusted sender with this permission was not established.
findings.evidence: At fixed commit 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, bus.rs:481-486 accepts the notification's channel_id and checks only for subscribers. Lines 498-502 fetch payload with WHERE id = $1, without checking the stored channel_id. Line 513 publishes using the notification's channel_id. ws.rs:836-844 sends the resulting payload without a further ownership check. The recovery path at bus.rs:539-554 instead routes by the stored channel_id.
findings.expected_behavior: The stored channel_id defines event ownership, as documented in rust/migrations/20260824090000_obs_dock_events.sql:47-48. An event for B must not reach A. The socket's history queries enforce this with WHERE channel_id = $1 at ws.rs:513-540.
findings.countermeasures: The inspected production writer constructs INSERT and NOTIFY from the same event.channel_id(), at rust/bin/tb-bot/src/obs_dock.rs:194-234, so its normal path cannot produce the mismatch. WebSocket authentication and channel scope run before subscription at ws.rs:463-497; clients cannot publish events through that socket. No public route to forge NOTIFY, lower-privilege database sender, or deployed NOTIFY privilege policy was established. This is therefore C, a conditional trust-boundary concern, not a demonstrated A vulnerability.

findings.claim: Kick and YouTube stream-key requests can wait indefinitely for their provider responses.
findings.failure_scenario: A connected partner requests a Kick or YouTube stream key with a valid, unexpired grant. The provider accepts the HTTPS request but never completes its response, for example by continuously sending whitespace in an unfinished JSON body. The dashboard request never reaches its error response and retains its task and upstream socket indefinitely. Concurrent retries can accumulate more pending requests.
findings.evidence: At fixed SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, the handler directly awaits plattform_stream_key_hinterlegen. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/plattform_connect.rs:530-554 awaits Kick konto or YouTube ziel. Both use api_get in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/plattform_oauth.rs:302-323, which constructs reqwest::Client::new() and awaits send and JSON decoding without any deadline. The locked reqwest 0.12.28 defaults both total and read timeouts to None. The reviewed router and production server add no enclosing request timeout.
findings.expected_behavior: An unavailable provider must terminate the stream-key operation within a finite external-call budget and use the existing StreamKeyStand::Fehlgeschlagen response, mapped to HTTP 502 at the finding file's lines 1685-1688, instead of holding the request indefinitely.
findings.countermeasures: Session authentication and CSRF restrict callers. Platform refresh has a 35-second enclosing deadline in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/platform_store.rs:339-344, but the subsequent konto/ziel lookup runs outside it. Relay requests have a 10-second timeout and 1 MiB body cap; Twitch requests have a 20-second timeout. Neither protects these Kick/YouTube API reads. Both platform branches were checked as twins. No runtime, network or proxy probes were performed.

findings.claim: Disconnect remains pending when the relay confirms that the destination is already absent.
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated streamer's destination is already absent, for example because its previous DELETE succeeded but the response was lost. A retry receives a successful response with the matching connection_generation and deleted=false. HttpRelayZiele returns Ok(false), but trennen returns RelayFehler without finishing the local disconnect. Repeated retries retain the pending generation and continue returning HTTP 502.
findings.evidence: At fixed revision 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/uplink.rs:1228 explicitly defines false as an absent destination. Lines 1303-1320 validate the acknowledgement generation before returning the deleted boolean. Lines 1507-1512 accept only Ok(true), skipping finish_uplink_disconnect. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-raid/src/target_generation.rs:102-117 persist disconnect_pending and reuse that generation on retry. The same rejection is present in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/plattform_connect.rs:719-724 for Kick and YouTube.
findings.expected_behavior: A successful, generation-matched DELETE confirming that no destination remains must allow the local disconnect to finish, whether this request removed a row or it was already absent. The generation module explicitly promises retryable completion after uncertain RPC results.
findings.countermeasures: Session-derived identity, CSRF protection, relay acknowledgement validation and local generation fencing remain necessary, but none resolves this boolean misinterpretation. Error responses and mismatched generations must still prevent completion. The Kick/YouTube twin was checked as targeted context, not claimed as full coverage of that file.

findings.claim: Delayed first listener startup silently loses events after the socket's initial replay.
findings.failure_scenario: The first socket completes its initial replay through event 100 while the first listener connection attempt fails or is delayed. Event 101 is then committed and notified before LISTEN succeeds. On its first successful connection, the listener initializes its watermark to MAX(id)=101 without replaying anything. Event 102 subsequently arrives normally, but the already-open socket never receives event 101 or a gap indication unless another recovery happens.
findings.evidence: bus.rs:393-405 only spawns startup. bus.rs:441-454 establishes LISTEN and then initializes an unknown watermark from the current MAX(id); replay at 458 occurs only when a watermark was already established. ws.rs:482-497 starts the listener without awaiting readiness and immediately permits subscription and initial replay. ws.rs:757-764 performs that initial replay once; subsequent database replay at 849-855 requires broadcast lag, which a notification missed before LISTEN does not generate.
findings.expected_behavior: Events produced after the connected socket's initial replay must be delivered live or explicitly identified as missing. ws.rs:15-19 documents a gap-free transition, and bus.rs:445-447 intends to exclude events preceding the process, not events generated while its first listener is starting.
findings.countermeasures: Subscription before replay protects only events already reaching the bus. Starting the listener before the upgrade callback does not wait for LISTEN. SQLx 0.9 eagerly reconnects established listeners, and the bus replays established-watermark failures, but neither protects the first-start unknown-watermark branch. Sources were verified against commit 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af.

findings.claim: Listener recovery silently omits missed events deleted by retention.
findings.failure_scenario: An active socket remains connected while its listener is unavailable for 25 minutes. The bot continues writing events, including event 101 shortly after the last delivered event 100. The retention worker deletes event 101 before the listener recovers. Recovery reads only surviving events, for example event 102, gets fewer than 500 rows, and returns success without any gap frame. The socket's history is incomplete but appears complete.
findings.evidence: bus.rs:536-558 queries surviving rows and treats a short result as successful completion without checking whether retention removed missed rows. Its only gap publication is the round-limit branch at 563-581. obs_dock.rs:48-60 sets 15-minute retention with five-minute cleanup ticks; 251-265 deletes expired rows. main.rs:1417-1422 enables this cleanup alongside the event writer. ws.rs:766-859 keeps sockets alive independently of listener recovery, and its session-check error branches at 401-416 allow them to remain connected during database errors.
findings.expected_behavior: Expired events need not be retained or replayed, but unrecoverable history must be announced to connected docks. ws.rs:42-53 explicitly promises a gap frame when the bus cannot deliver skipped rows and states that nothing is skipped silently; bus.rs:129-131 defines that frame for rows the bus can no longer supply.
findings.countermeasures: The retention policy itself is intentional. The defect is the missing client-visible loss indication. Replay limits produce a gap only after 20 full batches, so a retention-truncated or empty result bypasses that protection. Heartbeats do not trigger history recovery. The related live-notification branch at bus.rs:508-511 also silently ignores a row already removed by retention.

findings.claim: The first OBS dock can silently lose events between its initial replay and LISTEN activation.
findings.failure_scenario: After a dashboard process starts, its first authorized dock connects. Its initial replay finishes at ID 100 while the asynchronously spawned listener has not yet completed LISTEN. The bot commits and notifies event 101 during this interval. The listener subsequently activates LISTEN, reads MAX(id)=101 and treats that ID as already handled. Notification 101 was sent before subscription, so the connected dock never receives event 101 or a gap frame. No further traffic or reconnect is required for this failure.
findings.evidence: At baseline 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, bus.rs:393-405 starts the listener with tokio::spawn and provides no readiness synchronization. ws.rs:482-497 calls that method and proceeds to upgrade, subscribe and serve the socket; ws.rs:755-764 independently runs the initial replay. bus.rs:441-458 executes LISTEN and then initializes the unknown watermark to the current MAX(id), without publishing or replaying the intervening rows. The production writer commits INSERT before its separate pg_notify call at obs_dock.rs:205-236.
findings.expected_behavior: Events committed after a socket's initial replay must reach its live stream or produce an explicit gap indication. ws.rs:15-19 explicitly describes registration before replay as preventing a transition gap, and ws.rs:42-53 says skipped rows are never silent.
findings.countermeasures: Registration before replay protects only the broadcast subscription; it does not wait for the database subscription. Later listener reconnects do call luecke_nachziehen, but the first-start branch does not. Heartbeats and session checks do not periodically replay missing rows. Storage retention makes later manual recovery possible but does not correct the uninterrupted connection.

findings.claim: A one-connection database pool prevents the OBS listener from ever initializing.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure the dashboard's accepted database pool maximum as 1 and open an authorized OBS dock. PgListener reserves the only pool connection. Initialization then executes SELECT MAX(id) through the same pool, which cannot supply another connection. It times out, drops the listener and retries; every retry repeats the same sequence. The watermark remains unknown and the dock never receives live notifications.
findings.evidence: bus.rs:441 acquires PgListener from pool; bus.rs:448-451 immediately performs fetch_optional(pool) while that listener remains alive. SQLx 0.9.0 listener.rs:60-75 retains the acquired PoolConnection in the listener. The fixed workspace manifest pins SQLx 0.9.0. tb-config/src/lib.rs:125 accepts pool_max=1, tb-db/src/pool.rs:40-43 uses that maximum unchanged, and tb-dashboard/src/main.rs:400 and 476-483 pass this pool into the production router. lib.rs:1985-1992 attaches the bus with a clone of that same pool.
findings.expected_behavior: A pool size explicitly accepted by configuration must not make initialization structurally impossible. The live OBS listener must be able to obtain its required read connection, or the unsupported configuration must be rejected before serving docks.
findings.countermeasures: The default maximum of 10 avoids this specific case, but the configured minimum is 1 and there is no bus-level minimum or dedicated listener pool. Acquire timeouts bound each wait rather than resolving it. The retry loop at bus.rs:416-432 keeps using the same exhausted pool. Existing database-backed bus tests use pools with two connections.

findings.claim: OBS recovery emits a gap frame when exactly 10,000 rows are replayed and none were skipped.
findings.failure_scenario: During listener reconnection, set the existing watermark to 1,000 and retain exactly rows 1 through 10,000, with no concurrent writes. Recovery starts at zero and successfully processes twenty full batches of 500 rows. The table is now exhausted and MAX(id) equals the last processed ID, 10,000. Nevertheless the bus broadcasts a gap frame through ID 10,000 to every dock. An active channel with few rows avoids broadcast lag and receives this false indication despite complete delivery.
findings.evidence: bus.rs:72 and 78 set the limits to 500 rows and 20 rounds. bus.rs:536-559 returns early only for a short batch, so an exactly full final batch falls through. bus.rs:565-580 reads MAX(id) and unconditionally publishes BusRahmen::luecke(ziel), even when ziel equals zeiger and uebersprungen is zero. ws.rs:827-834 forwards this frame directly; gap frames are not suppressed by event deduplication.
findings.expected_behavior: A gap frame denotes rows the bus actually skipped, as specified by BusRahmen.json at bus.rs:129-131 and the recovery contract at bus.rs:524-526. Exhausting the table exactly at the batch limit must not report missing history.
findings.countermeasures: The twenty-round cap is intentional for genuinely oversized gaps, but no remaining-row or ziel>zeiger check distinguishes exact exhaustion. The analogous websocket replay path already checks ziel<=buch.anker() and returns without a gap at ws.rs:709-711. The existing bus pagination test covers 1,013 rows, not the exact 10,000-row boundary.

findings.claim: First listener startup can silently lose events committed after a socket finishes replay.
findings.failure_scenario: With the event bus enabled, the first authenticated socket registers and completes its history query while the spawned PgListener is still connecting. A new event then commits and sends NOTIFY before LISTEN is established. The listener subsequently initializes its watermark to MAX(id), including that event, without replaying it. The event reaches neither the socket's completed replay nor its live stream, and no gap frame is sent.
findings.evidence: listener_sicherstellen only spawns a task (393-405). horchen establishes LISTEN and, on first startup, stores MAX(id) without calling luecke_nachziehen (441-459). The WebSocket handler starts the listener without awaiting readiness, then registers and replays in its independent upgrade task. PgObsDockSink commits INSERT and subsequently sends NOTIFY in separate statements.
findings.expected_behavior: The gateway's subscribe-before-replay contract explicitly prevents transition gaps. Events committed after the initial replay must be delivered live or recovered with an explicit gap indication.
findings.countermeasures: The registration mutex protects the in-memory broadcast subscription, not PostgreSQL LISTEN readiness. Auth and channel scoping do not serialize startup with replay. Normal heartbeats do not perform another history query.

findings.claim: Recovery followed by queued NOTIFY messages can deliver the same event twice after socket deduplication IDs are evicted.
findings.failure_scenario: After reconnect establishes LISTEN, 9000 new rows alternating between two already-open channels commit and notify before recovery finishes. Recovery publishes these rows first. Each fast socket drains approximately 250 events per 500-row batch and receives 4500 distinct events, evicting its earliest 404 IDs from the 4096-entry deduplication set. Recovery finishes below its 10000-row cap. When the listener subsequently consumes the queued notifications, the evicted IDs pass live() again and are sent a second time on the same connection.
findings.evidence: LISTEN precedes recovery (441-458), while notification reception follows recovery (461-465). luecke_nachziehen can publish 20 batches of 500 rows (538-555). GESENDET_FENSTER is only 4096 (638), and merken removes earlier IDs (747-752). live accepts an evicted ID above vor_verbindung (699-704); the socket sends accepted frames.
findings.expected_behavior: The delivery documentation promises duplicate-free delivery within a connection and requires the remembered-ID window to cover everything the bus can deliver twice (631-661).
findings.countermeasures: The unique dedupe_key index prevents duplicate database rows, not repeated distribution of one row. The compile-time checks cover the 1000-ID lookback, 256-frame broadcast buffer and 200-row query size, but not the full recovery span. Draining each per-channel batch avoids Lagged, and staying below the recovery cap avoids a gap frame that would suppress the queued duplicates.

findings.claim: A failed fetch of a late low-ID notification is silently omitted from recovery outside the 1000-ID lookback.
findings.failure_scenario: Notifications from other channels advance the global watermark to 5000. A delayed concurrent writer then notifies a recent, retained row with ID 3999 for an open quiet channel. The listener consumes that notification, but its payload SELECT fails once. Reconnection succeeds and starts recovery at 4000, so WHERE id > 4000 excludes row 3999. Its consumed notification is not resent, and the quiet socket receives neither the event nor a gap frame.
findings.evidence: The payload SELECT propagates errors before updating the watermark (498-507). Earlier higher IDs remain in the global fetch_max watermark, including notifications for channels without receivers (486-495). Recovery subtracts only NACHZUG_RUECKGRIFF and filters on that resulting numeric ID (536-549). The producer uses independently committed INSERT and NOTIFY statements, and the BIGSERIAL schema does not enforce commit or notification order.
findings.expected_behavior: The error-handling comment at 503-506 explicitly promises recovery of the row whose SELECT failed. The module also requires out-of-order IDs not to be silently discarded.
findings.countermeasures: Updating the watermark only after a successful SELECT does not undo an earlier higher watermark. The two-second producer timeout limits duration, not the global sequence-ID distance across channels. Retention does not remove the recent row in this scenario. The quiet channel does not experience broadcast lag, and the recovery cap is not reached, so neither gap mechanism compensates.

findings.claim: Backpressured OBS writes bypass the idle timeout and six-socket cap.
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated dock stops reading while its channel continues producing events. Once TCP buffers fill, the awaited send remains pending. The socket no longer polls heartbeat, session checks or its eviction receiver. Opening replacement docks can leave more than six actual socket tasks and file descriptors alive, despite the bus reporting only six registered sockets. A peer keeping TCP open with a zero receive window need not cause a transport error.
findings.evidence: At fixed SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, ws.rs:781-861 awaits writes inside selected branch bodies rather than racing them against cancellation or a deadline. The same unbounded writes occur during replay at 631-639 and 687-693, gap notification at 728-735, and shutdown at 870-877. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/obs/bus.rs:298-310 removes the oldest registry entry and merely sends its oneshot cancellation; it does not abort the task.
findings.expected_behavior: The 120-second idle limit in ws.rs:112-113 and the explicitly hard six-socket limit in bus.rs:57-61 must still terminate unresponsive sockets when their writes are blocked.
findings.countermeasures: Authentication and channel binding restrict access. The broadcast buffer and delivery bookkeeping are bounded. The biased select prioritizes cancellation, but only between completed branch bodies; it cannot interrupt an awaited send. Eviction is cooperative, and SocketWaechter cleanup only runs when the socket function exits. Production proxy and OS timeout settings were not inspected.

findings.claim: Stalled OBS database replies suspend heartbeat and socket eviction indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario: An established database connection stops returning replies without closing, for example when the database backend or intervening connection is stalled. An open dock reaches its periodic session check and waits on that connection. It then stops delivering events, responding to client pings, enforcing the 120-second idle limit and receiving eviction requests. Initial replay and lag recovery can enter the same stuck state while retaining pool connections.
findings.evidence: ws.rs:803 awaits waechter.gueltig() inside the select branch. Its session lookups at 384, 394 and 407 reach /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/auth/session.rs:1993-2014, which awaits fetch_optional without a deadline. Replay likewise awaits fetch_all at ws.rs:524-542 before entering the live loop at 762, and again inside it at 854. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-db-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-db/src/pool.rs is not used as evidence; the reviewed pool implementation is /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-db/src/pool.rs:10-11,20-58: production connect uses read_only=false, sets acquisition deadlines, and does not bound execution of established queries.
findings.expected_behavior: Database outages must not freeze the socket lifecycle. ws.rs:372-373 explicitly intends database errors to leave the dock running, and its idle and eviction guards must remain effective while database work is outstanding.
findings.countermeasures: Pool acquisition and connection establishment are bounded, but those deadlines do not bound replies on an acquired connection. The five-second session cache cannot protect recurring checks, and durable-session lookup has no cache. Error handling returns true only after the query actually returns an error. A server-side statement timeout cannot guarantee a client deadline when the backend or connection cannot deliver its reply. No database or network probes were performed.

findings.claim: Die Sechs-Socket-Grenze lässt blockierte, verdrängte OBS-Sockets weiterleben.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein angemeldeter Partner öffnet sechs OBS-Sockets und liest anschließend keine Daten mehr. Sobald die Ausgabepuffer gefüllt sind, warten die Socket-Aufgaben in send().await. Weitere Verbindungen entfernen jeweils den ältesten Eintrag aus der Busliste und senden dessen Abbruchsignal, unterbrechen aber nicht das wartende Schreiben. Wiederholt der Partner dies, bleiben mehr als sechs tatsächliche Verbindungen samt Aufgaben und Speicher bestehen, obwohl socket_anzahl() höchstens sechs meldet.
findings.evidence: Basis 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. Im angegebenen bus.rs entfernen Zeilen 298-300 den Eintrag bereits vor dem bloßen oneshot-Signal in Zeile 310. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/obs/ws.rs:785-790 verarbeitet dieses Signal nur im äußeren select!. Das Schreiben in Zeile 844 wartet dagegen innerhalb eines ausgewählten Zweigs ohne Zeitgrenze oder konkurrierende Abbruchprüfung. Ebenso wartet der anfängliche Nachlauf in Zeile 762 außerhalb der Abbruchprüfung; dessen Schreibstellen liegen in Zeilen 632-635 und 687-690. Die Axum-Sink-Implementierung delegiert poll_flush ohne eigene Zeitgrenze. Der Bus-Test in Zeilen 849-865 belegt nur die begrenzte Liste und das versendete Signal, nicht das Ende der Socket-Aufgabe.
findings.expected_behavior: bus.rs:57-61 bezeichnet sechs ausdrücklich als harte Obergrenze offener Sockets. Eine siebte Verbindung muss den ältesten Socket tatsächlich beenden, auch wenn dessen Ausgabe blockiert.
findings.countermeasures: Die Anmeldung erfordert eine gültige Sitzung und beschränkt Partner auf ihren eigenen Kanal. Broadcast-Puffer und Merkliste sind pro Verbindung begrenzt. Der 120-Sekunden-Leerlaufdeckel und das priorisierte Abbruchsignal helfen nur, solange die Aufgabe zum äußeren select! zurückkehrt. Auch der abschließende Close-Versand wartet ohne Zeitgrenze. Eine zusätzliche externe Proxy-Zeitgrenze ist im geprüften Router nicht belegt; keine Betriebsprobes durchgeführt.

findings.claim: Der OBS-Listener kann mit dem erlaubten Ein-Verbindungs-Pool niemals starten.
findings.failure_scenario: Mit der gültigen Einstellung database.pool_max=1 startet die erste OBS-Verbindung den Listener. PgListener belegt die einzige Poolverbindung dauerhaft. Anschließend versucht die Wasserstandsabfrage, eine zweite Verbindung aus demselben Pool zu erwerben, und endet nach acquire_timeout mit PoolTimedOut. Jeder Wiederholungsversuch erzeugt denselben Zustand; der Listener erreicht seine Empfangsschleife nie und liefert keine Live-Ereignisse.
findings.evidence: Basis 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. bus.rs:441 erstellt PgListener aus pool; Zeilen 448-452 führen danach SELECT MAX(id) ebenfalls über pool aus, während listener für die Empfangsschleife in Zeile 462 weiterlebt. findings.claim: Another account's access-session cookie bypasses revocation of an OBS socket's authenticated session.
findings.failure_scenario: Connect to channel A with a valid twitch_dash_session for A and a valid twitch_dash_session_partner for account B, using the User-Agent matching B's access session. The upgrade authenticates A through the short-lived session. Revoke A's session while leaving B's session valid. Subsequent checks receive Ok(None) for A, then Ok(Some(B)) for the durable cookie and keep delivering channel A's events, although neither remaining session authorizes channel A.
findings.evidence: At fixed SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, auth/level.rs:353-366 authenticates the short-lived partner cookie first. obs/ws.rs:343-353 retains both cookies without retaining the authenticated Twitch ID. Its checks at 383-403 discard the loaded PartnerSession and accept either account. socket_bedienen keeps the original channel_id and closes only when this boolean becomes false at 802-805. auth/session.rs:1878-1953 loads the durable cookie's own identity independently; invalidate_session at 1506-1528 removes the revoked session but does not close the socket directly.
findings.expected_behavior: Session revalidation must retain authorization for the socket's bound channel. A fallback session for another Twitch ID must not keep that channel readable after its authorized session is revoked.
findings.countermeasures: Initial channel scoping and numeric identity validation correctly bind the upgrade to A. The durable-session User-Agent check protects device binding, not channel identity. Neither loader compares its returned account with the socket's original account, and HTTP middleware does not reauthorize individual WebSocket frames. No runtime probes were performed.

findings.claim: A stale partner cookie prematurely closes an OBS socket authenticated by a valid master session.

The synthetic partner_cookie_schlaegt_master_cookie test at 1136-1144 checks construction only, not authentication fallback.
findings.expected_behavior: An OBS socket authenticated through a currently valid master session must not report session expiration because an unrelated, already-invalid partner cookie accompanied the request.

findings.claim: OBS listener startup can silently lose events after replay but before PostgreSQL LISTEN becomes active.
findings.failure_scenario: After dashboard startup, the first dock completes its database replay while the newly spawned listener has not yet completed LISTEN. An event is inserted and its pg_notify completes in that interval. The notification has no listening consumer. The listener subsequently initializes its watermark from MAX(id), including that event, and enters live operation without replaying it. The dock remains connected, receives later events normally, and receives neither the missed event nor a gap notification.
findings.evidence: obs/ws.rs:484 invokes listener_sicherstellen synchronously, then 496-497 registers and serves the socket. bus.rs:393-405 only spawns the listener task and exposes no readiness barrier. Socket replay finishes at ws.rs:762-764. bus.rs:441-455 activates LISTEN later and initializes an unknown watermark with the current MAX(id), skipping initial gap recovery. Subsequent socket replay occurs only for broadcast Lagged at ws.rs:849-855, which a notification never received by the bus cannot generate. obs_dock.rs:205-238 confirms the producer persists the event and sends a one-shot pg_notify.
findings.expected_behavior: The documented replay-to-live transition at obs/ws.rs:15-19 must not silently omit persisted events. Listener startup must establish coverage of events committed after the socket's replay snapshot.
findings.countermeasures: Subscribing to the in-process broadcast before replay only protects events already reaching that broadcast. Listener reconnect recovery covers an established watermark but is skipped on first startup. Existing socket tests mostly inject a database-free bus; the full-router test explicitly checks upgrade and replay rather than live listener startup at ws.rs:1804-1817. Source drift checks were clean; no builds, tests, or network probes were run.

findings.claim: OBS sockets perpetually renew centrally revoked admin sessions.
findings.failure_scenario: A socket connects using a valid master_dash_session M. The central broker subsequently revokes M, or its centrally approved expiry passes, while its local Twitch mirror remains present. The client keeps responding to heartbeats. Each minute the socket reloads only the local mirror, which slides its expiry forward by fourteen days and periodically persists that extension. The socket therefore continues reading its subscribed channel indefinitely rather than ending at the local fallback deadline.

findings.expected_behavior: A centrally invalidated session must not obtain unbounded continued access through a renewable local mirror. Even the deliberately deferred revocation policy documented at /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/obs/ws.rs:301-316 promises access only until local expiry, not perpetual renewal without central approval.

Local session loading checks database and payload expiry, and a logout through this Twitch service explicitly deletes the local mirror. Auch der 120-Sekunden-Leerlaufdeckel wird in derselben blockierten Schleife geprüft und kann deshalb nicht helfen. Die Bus-Sperre begrenzt die Registrierungsmenge, nicht die weiterlebenden verdrängten Socket-Tasks.

findings.claim: viewer-overlap always substitutes one for the own-channel audience count because its total-query placeholders are misnumbered.

Lines 148-155 silently discard the PostgreSQL error and use 1. The independently bound overlap query can succeed, and lines 183-195 compute percentages using this fabricated denominator.

findings.claim: A different partner's durable session keeps a revoked channel socket open.
findings.failure_scenario: A WebSocket upgrade carries a valid short session for partner A and a separately issued, fingerprint-matching durable session for partner B. Authentication selects A and subscribes to A's channel. After A's short session is invalidated, load_partner_session returns None, but load_partner_access_session returns partner B. The minute check therefore continues returning true, and the existing socket keeps receiving A's events although no remaining credential authorizes A.
findings.evidence: At the fixed revision, auth/level.rs:353-393 selects the short session before the durable session. ws.rs:343-353 retains both cookies but not the authenticated Twitch ID. ws.rs:383-395 accepts either loader's Some result without comparing identities. The subscription remains bound to the original channel in ws.rs:496-497 and 740-745. auth_login.rs:738-740 invalidates the short session independently; session.rs:1511-1527 deletes that session and clears its caches. session.rs:1943-1952 returns the durable session's own partner identity, which the watcher discards.
findings.expected_behavior: Session revalidation must preserve the original channel authorization. A fallback credential for B cannot keep an A-bound socket authorized after all credentials for A become invalid; the socket should close with SessionAbgelaufen.
findings.countermeasures: Initial channel ownership is enforced by kanal_freigabe, and durable sessions check their own partner membership and User-Agent fingerprint. Those protections authorize the initial A session or the independent B session, not B's continued access to A. The failure requires successful database reads, so the intentional database-outage fallback is irrelevant.

findings.claim: Admin OBS channel resolution selects historical owners and ignores verified actor IDs.
findings.failure_scenario: The partner table contains an older archived row with login foo and Twitch ID 111, plus a newer active row with the same login and ID 222. An admin requests /obs/ws?streamer=foo. kanal_kennung selects ID 111 because it orders all statuses by ascending id. The socket reads and subscribes to the historical account instead of the current account. The same wrong result occurs when the admin actor already has verified identity foo/222.
findings.evidence: ws.rs:237-246 preserves IDs only for DashboardAuthLevel::Partner. Its fallback query at 248-254 filters by login, ignores status, and uses ORDER BY id LIMIT 1. ws.rs:467-497 uses that returned ID for both replay and subscription. baseline_schema.sql:2573-2575 enforces login and user-ID uniqueness only for active rows, so the archived/active pair is permitted. auth/level.rs:280-285 and 304-309 preserve verified admin actor IDs; auth/streamer_scope.rs:186-196 explicitly retains them for an admin's own target.
findings.expected_behavior: An admin request for the current channel must resolve to its current platform identity. A verified own-channel actor ID must not be replaced by an older account that previously held the same login.
findings.countermeasures: The initial scope guard permits an admin to select a channel but does not repair the identity lookup. Active-only uniqueness does not exclude historical duplicates. Partner sockets avoid this through their session-ID fast path. The moderation-settings resolver at 103-106 has a related unqualified historical login lookup; only that targeted counterpart was inspected.

findings.claim: The first OBS socket can silently miss events while its PostgreSQL listener starts.
findings.failure_scenario: After dashboard startup, the first dock connects while the spawned listener is still acquiring its connection or establishing LISTEN. The socket subscribes to the in-process bus and finishes its database replay. An event is then inserted and notified before PostgreSQL LISTEN becomes active. Its notification has no listener, and the eventual initial MAX(id) includes that event. The healthy listener never replays it, so the open dock misses the event without a gap frame.
findings.evidence: ws.rs:484 starts the listener without awaiting readiness, then 486-497 opens and registers the socket; 757-764 performs replay immediately. bus.rs:393-405 only sets a flag and spawns a task. bus.rs:441-454 establishes LISTEN asynchronously and, on its first start, initializes the watermark to MAX(id) without catch-up. The producer in bin/tb-bot/src/obs_dock.rs:205-236 inserts and then sends pg_notify. Subsequent healthy operation in bus.rs:461-470 only receives notifications; socket heartbeat and session ticks do not poll for missed events. lib.rs:1970-1972 confirms this lazy startup is the production lifecycle.
findings.expected_behavior: Events created after a dock's replay snapshot must be captured by its live subscription or explicitly reported as missing. ws.rs:15-19 promises that subscribing before replay prevents this transition gap, and 42-53 promises that skipped events are not silent.
findings.countermeasures: Subscribing before replay protects against overlap with an already running bus, but does not establish PostgreSQL listener readiness. Replay on a later reconnect can recover the event, but does not correct the currently open socket. Existing socket tests mostly use a database-free bus; ws.rs:1810-1817 explicitly says the full-router test does not verify the live path.

findings.claim: Stale partner cookies incorrectly expire master-authenticated OBS sockets.
findings.failure_scenario: A request carries an invalidated short partner cookie, no valid durable partner cookie, and a valid master_dash_session. The authentication extractor rejects the stale partner credential, accepts the master session, and successfully upgrades the owner's dock. SessionWaechter nevertheless chooses its Partner variant merely because the stale cookie exists. At the first minute check it returns false and closes the valid master-authenticated socket with SessionAbgelaufen.

findings.claim: Ein blockierter Best-effort-Backfill hängt Audience-Insights ohne Zeitgrenze und kann den gemeinsamen DB-Pool vollständig belegen.
findings.failure_scenario: PostgreSQL läuft mit statement_timeout=0. Eine offene Transaktion hält eine Zeilensperre auf einem twitch_session_chatters-Datensatz einer abgeschlossenen Session; dessen last_seen_at ist NULL oder älter als die vorhandene letzte Chat-Nachricht. Bei zehn parallelen solchen Requests und der Standard-Poolgröße zehn bleiben alle Verbindungen belegt; weitere Dashboard-DB-Zugriffe scheitern nach dem Erwerbs-Timeout, während die ursprünglichen Requests nicht abgeschlossen werden.

findings.expected_behavior: Der laut audience.rs:575 ausdrücklich nur Best-effort gedachte Backfill darf die Insights-Antwort bei einer blockierten Datenbankoperation nicht unbegrenzt verhindern.
