C, weil die angemessene Budgetierung und der Umbau des ausdrücklich als vollständiger Snapshot definierten Loaders eine Implementierungsentscheidung erfordern; ein stilles LIMIT würde das Produktverhalten verändern.

findings.claim: Audience-sharing can return Jaccard similarity above 1 when a chatter arrives between its count queries.

findings.claim: Internal chatter-history queries have no deadline and can exhaust the shared dashboard connection pool.
findings.failure_scenario: With PostgreSQL's default statement_timeout=0, another transaction retains an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on twitch_live_state. A valid loopback request with the internal credential blocks in laufende_session. Repeating the request up to the configured pool capacity occupies every connection indefinitely; unrelated dashboard queries then fail their pool-acquisition deadlines. The history requests never reach the documented unavailable response while the lock persists.
findings.evidence: The handler awaits laufende_session at line 118; its SELECT at lines 161-174 has neither a query deadline nor an enclosing timeout. The subsequent analytics lookup at lines 133-140 has the same omission. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/bin/tb-dashboard/src/main.rs:400 uses tb_db::connect, whose /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-db/src/pool.rs:10-11 selects read_only=false. That pool sets an acquisition deadline at line 44, but applies the 20-second statement timeout only inside the read_only branch at lines 47-53. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:1941-1960 and 2219 wire this internal route to the shared pool without a timeout layer.
findings.expected_behavior: The route documents HTTP 503 when evaluation does not respond at lines 73-75 and implements that response at lines 185-190. A stalled database operation should terminate within a finite request/query deadline rather than reserve shared pool capacity until the database recovers.
findings.countermeasures: Loopback plus credential validation and LOGINS_MAX=50 protect access and result size, not query duration. Pool acquire_timeout bounds waiting for a connection, not execution after acquiring one. The readonly-pool statement timeout is real but does not apply to this pool. A separately configured PostgreSQL timeout could bound lock waiting; deployed database settings and external relay-client behavior were not probed. The same unbounded-await pattern was checked in engagement-mode and experimental analytics handlers.

GET /twitch/api/v2/viewer-directory?streamer=recycled&days=3650 returns user 111's historical viewers, counts and timestamps. viewer-detail also accepts viewers found only in those historical sessions, and viewer-segments includes those viewers.
findings.evidence: Reviewed at fixed SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. The directory and segments handlers resolve the authenticated login, then call fetch_window_viewer_rows, whose SQL at lines 196-210 filters sc.streamer_login and time but never s.twitch_user_id. Detail repeats this at lines 598-611. Historical ownership is already stored: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/migrations/20260802140000_kanal_id_spalten_historientabellen.sql:28-60 adds the session Twitch ID and index. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-monitoring/src/streamer_login.rs:359-375 explicitly renames only open sessions, preserving completed sessions' old logins. Routes are registered as GET endpoints in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:974-985.
findings.expected_behavior: An authenticated partner's channel history must belong to their verified Twitch user ID. Receiving another account's former login must not grant access to that account's viewer analytics.
findings.countermeasures: Session loading authenticates the numerical user ID, partner_status_gate requires an active partner, extended_gate requires Plus, and resolve_streamer_scope rejects a different requested login. None binds the selected historical rows to that user ID. The scenario supplies the attacker's own valid Plus entitlement, so it does not depend on the separate billing defect. The watch-time handler has the same login-only session selection in its analytics loader, but its UPDATE backfill and database write privileges can prevent delivery; the demonstrated disclosure here uses the SELECT-only viewer endpoints. No live requests or database probes were performed.

findings.claim: Viewer plan gates accept another Twitch user's paid subscription after login reuse.
findings.failure_scenario: User 111 has an active paid Stripe subscription whose customer_reference is 'recycled', then changes their Twitch login. User 222 later becomes an active partner under 'recycled', with no paid subscription and no active manual override or trial. Their authenticated request to viewer-directory, viewer-detail or viewer-segments passes the Plus gate because the resolver selects user 111's subscription by the reused login. The attacker thereby obtains paid viewer features without their own entitlement.
findings.evidence: The assigned handlers call extended_gate at lines 258, 553 and 920. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/auth/mod.rs:164-219 passes the authenticated login and ID through stufe_fuer_auth. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/stufe.rs:133-139 uses the non-identity-bound resolve_plan_snapshot. In /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/plan.rs:535-556, subscription lookup accepts customer_reference matching the login OR the user ID, without verifying ownership of the login reference. The alternative resolver at lines 355-363 and 503-533 already rejects conflicting ID-to-login mappings. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-monitoring/src/streamer_login.rs:58-163,341-394 does not rewrite billing subscriptions on rename. The assigned watch-time handler at line 51 similarly uses the unbound resolver and additionally discards the authenticated user ID.
findings.expected_behavior: Paid access must be determined by the authenticated Twitch identity. A subscription associated with a former holder of the same login must not entitle the current holder.
findings.countermeasures: Authenticated numeric IDs, current partner lookup, active-partner middleware and the streamer scope guard prevent account impersonation, but do not validate subscription-reference ownership. The normal resolver prioritizes an own manual override when one exists; the scenario deliberately has no active own override and an expired or already-consumed trial. Fail-closed database-error handling is irrelevant because the foreign subscription lookup succeeds. The primary viewer routes perform SELECT queries, so dashboard read-only privileges do not prevent this gate bypass. No live configuration, secrets, database state or network responses were inspected.

findings.claim: Wartende Viewer-SQL-Abfragen können alle Dashboard-Verbindungen ohne Ausführungsfrist belegen.
findings.failure_scenario: Bei statement_timeout=0 und lock_timeout=0 hält eine andere Transaktion eine ACCESS-EXCLUSIVE-Sperre auf twitch_session_chatters. Zehn berechtigte parallele Viewer-Abfragen können dann sämtliche Verbindungen des standardmäßig zehn Verbindungen großen Dashboard-Pools belegen. Weitere Dashboard-Abfragen scheitern beim Erwerb einer Verbindung, während die ursprünglichen Abfragen bis zur Freigabe der Sperre weiter warten.
findings.evidence: Am festen SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af wartet fetch_window_viewer_rows mit fetch_all(...).await ohne Deadline (196-213). Dashboard main verwendet tb_db::connect (400); dessen normaler Modus setzt nur die Verbindungsbeschaffungsfrist. statement_timeout=20000 wird ausschließlich im nicht verwendeten Read-only-Modus gesetzt (pool.rs:20-55). Die geprüften Router-Schichten enthalten keine Ausführungsfrist. Derselbe fehlende Schutz besteht bei viewer-detail, viewer-segments und dem Watch-Time-Aufruf (watch_time.rs:84-85), dessen Implementierung eine Verbindung während mehrerer Transaktionsabfragen hält.
findings.expected_behavior: Blockierte Analytics-Abfragen sollten nach einer definierten Frist abbrechen und ihre Pool-Verbindung freigeben. Für den normalen Dashboard-Pool ist allerdings keine verbindliche Ausführungsfrist belegt; deren Festlegung und Abbruchverhalten bleiben deshalb Klasse C.
findings.countermeasures: Authentifizierung, Plan-Gate und Kanalbindung begrenzen die berechtigten Aufrufer, nicht die Wartezeit. acquire_timeout begrenzt nur den Erwerb einer Verbindung. Eine extern gesetzte PostgreSQL-Ausführungsfrist könnte das Szenario verhindern; tatsächliche Datenbank-, DSN- und Proxy-Einstellungen wurden entsprechend dem Auftrag nicht untersucht.

findings.claim: Die Seitengröße begrenzt den Speicherbedarf des Viewer-Verzeichnisses nicht.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein Dashboard-Prozess mit 512 MiB Speicherbudget verarbeitet page=1&per_page=10&days=3650 für einen Kanal mit einer Million verschiedenen, nicht ausgeschlossenen Zuschauern im Zeitfenster. Vor der Ausgabe der zehn Einträge werden sämtliche Zuschauer und ihre JSON-Objekte gleichzeitig materialisiert. Die Millionen JSON-Felder, Schlüssel, Metadaten und Login-Kopien überschreiten dieses Budget; der Prozess kann wegen Speichermangels abbrechen. Eine Suchanfrage nach einem einzelnen Zuschauer verhindert diese Materialisierung ebenfalls nicht.
findings.evidence: fetch_window_viewer_rows lädt alle gruppierten Zuschauer ohne LIMIT (196-225). Das Verzeichnis erzeugt anschließend all_logins und Metadaten für die gesamte Population (320-345), lädt sämtliche Zuschauer-Kanal-Gruppen, obwohl nur drei Kanäle je Zuschauer verwendet werden (348-375), und baut vollständige JSON-Objekte für alle Zuschauer (381-445). Suche und Filter erfolgen erst bei 459-478, die Seitenauswahl erst bei 506-512. viewer-segments verwendet denselben unbeschränkten Loader (941) und hält ebenfalls populationsgroße JSON-Sammlungen (958-999). Dies ist ein statisch abgeleitetes Fehlerszenario, kein beobachteter Produktionsausfall.
findings.expected_behavior: Ein kleiner Seitenabruf sollte nicht die gesamte historische Zuschauerpopulation als JSON im Prozess halten müssen. Eine speicherschonende Umsetzung muss die bestehenden globalen Zusammenfassungen, Filter und Sortierungen bewahren; dafür ist eine bewusste Änderung der Abfragestruktur erforderlich, daher Klasse C.
findings.countermeasures: per_page ist auf 10-100 und days auf 1-3650 begrenzt. Beide Grenzen beschränken jedoch weder die Zuschaueranzahl noch die geladenen Kanalgruppen. Plan-Gate und Kanalbindung bleiben wirksam, verhindern aber große berechtigte Datenbestände nicht. Ein verbindliches Speicherbudget oder eine maximale Population ist in den geprüften Quellen nicht belegt.

findings.claim: Watch-Time übersieht Analytics-Pläne, die über die Twitch-ID zugeordnet sind.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein aktiver Partner mit Login 'host' und Twitch-ID '42' besitzt ein gültiges Plus-Abo mit customer_reference='42', aber kein zusätzliches loginbasiertes Abo oder Override. Bei days=30 werden trotz Plus nur Daten des letzten abgeschlossenen Streams geladen; ältere Streams und der Vorperiodenvergleich fehlen.
findings.evidence: resolve_read_window übergibt resolve_plan_snapshot(pool, streamer, "") und verwirft die vorhandene Partner-ID. Im festen SHA prüft plan.rs:545-546 ID-basierte Abos ausschließlich bei nichtleerem user_id. plan.rs:65-70 gibt Plus das analytics-Entitlement. watch_time.rs:33-38 reduziert den dadurch fälschlich ermittelten Free-Plan auf last_stream. tb-analytics/src/watch_time.rs:50-59 und 262-264 setzen dieses verkürzte Fenster tatsächlich um.
findings.expected_behavior: Ein gültiges Analytics-Abo desselben authentifizierten Twitch-Kontos muss das volle angefragte Fenster erhalten. Das belegen watch_time.rs:8-10 und der ausdrücklich ID- und loginfähige Planresolver in plan.rs:496-498.
findings.countermeasures: Admins umgehen die Planprüfung; loginbasierte Abos funktionieren. resolve_streamer_scope validiert die Partner-ID und den eigenen Login, reicht die ID aber nicht an diesen Resolver weiter. partner_status_gate verändert keine Aboreferenzen. Die Handler-Tests prüfen keine ID-basierte Berechtigung. Gezielter Zwilling: handlers/overview.rs:439 verwirft ebenfalls die ID; dort wurde nur der Resolverausschnitt gelesen.

findings.claim: Die first_seen-Sortierung des Viewer-Verzeichnisses sortiert nach Sessions.
findings.failure_scenario: Viewer A wurde vor zehn Tagen erstmals gesehen und hat zehn Sessions; Viewer B wurde vor einem Tag erstmals gesehen und hat eine Session. Ein Request mit sort=first_seen&order=desc liefert A vor B, obwohl B den späteren firstSeen-Zeitpunkt hat.
findings.evidence: viewers.rs:282 erkennt first_seen und setzt den Sortierschlüssel auf firstSeen. Die Vergleichsfunktion in 483-489 behandelt diesen Schlüssel nicht und fällt auf totalSessions zurück. Der reale Frontend-Aufrufer Viewers.tsx:751 wählt first_seen; api/analytics.ts:448-449 übermittelt sort und order unverändert.
findings.expected_behavior: Der ausdrücklich unterstützte first_seen-Schlüssel muss firstSeen vergleichen, nicht totalSessions. Belege sind die Parametermapping-Zeile 282, das ausgegebene firstSeen-Feld in 430 und ViewerSortField in types/analytics.ts:1149.
findings.countermeasures: Authentifizierung und Scope-Guard beschränken den Zugriff, ändern den Sortierschlüssel aber nicht. Es gibt keine vorgeschaltete Umschreibung im gelesenen API-Aufrufer. Die Tests der Primärdatei decken diese Sortierung nicht ab.

findings.claim: Große gültige Seitenzahlen lassen den Viewer-Directory-Offset überlaufen.
findings.failure_scenario: Bei 100 passenden Viewern wird page=368934881474191034&per_page=50 angefragt. Die Multiplikation ergibt 2^64+34. Im Release-Build läuft der i64-Offset auf 34 über und liefert Viewer 35 bis 84 statt einer leeren Seite. Bei aktivierten Overflow-Prüfungen panikt der Handler.
findings.evidence: DirectoryQuery akzeptiert page als i64. Zeile 288 setzt nur eine Untergrenze. Zeile 507 multipliziert (page-1)*per_page ungeprüft vor dem usize-Cast, und 510-511 verwenden den resultierenden Offset. rust/Cargo.toml:128-130 aktiviert keine Overflow-Prüfung für das Release-Profil.
findings.expected_behavior: Eine Seite weit außerhalb der Ergebnisanzahl muss leer bleiben oder als ungültig abgewiesen werden. Sie darf weder vorhandene frühere Seiten erneut liefern noch den Request durch einen Arithmetic-Panic abbrechen.
findings.countermeasures: per_page wird auf 10 bis 100 begrenzt, page jedoch nicht nach oben. Die konkrete Seitenzahl ist ein gültiger positiver i64-Wert. Extended-Gate und Scope-Guard begrenzen die berechtigten Aufrufer, verhindern diesen Eingabefall aber nicht.

findings.claim: Viewer-Segmente zählen ausschließlich im Heimkanal vorhandene Zuschauer nicht als exklusiv.
findings.failure_scenario: Im gewählten Fenster gibt es genau einen echten Viewer, der nur den Heimkanal besucht hat. viewer-segments liefert exclusiveViewersPct=0. Gleichzeitig liefert viewer-directory exclusiveViewers=1. Im Frontend steht deshalb 0 % exklusiv neben einem vollständig exklusiven Diagramm.
findings.evidence: Die Cross-Channel-Query in 1094-1107 schließt den Heimkanal aus. Für den beschriebenen Viewer entsteht dadurch keine Ergebniszeile. Die Schleife in 1115-1121 zählt ausschließlich vorhandene cc_rows, sodass exclusive_count bei null bleibt, während der Nenner total=1 ist. Viewers.tsx:498-505 nutzt Directory-Zahlen für das Diagramm und 636 die Segment-Prozentzahl für dessen Beschriftung.
findings.expected_behavior: Ein Viewer ohne andere Kanäle muss als exklusiv zählen. Das ist im Kommentar 1084-1086 ausdrücklich beschrieben und in der Directory-Klassifikation 395 und 415-418 implementiert.
findings.countermeasures: Bot- und Streamer-Selbstausschluss greifen bereits beim Laden der Viewer und beseitigen den echten Viewer nicht. Die Regression 1573-1629 prüft einen Viewer mit einem anderen Kanal, aber keinen Viewer ohne andere Kanäle. Für fehlende cc_rows existiert kein Nullkanal-Fallback.

findings.claim: Viewer-Verzeichnis und Segmente widersprechen sich bei Cross-Channel-Kennzahlen.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein echter Viewer besucht den Heimkanal und genau einen anderen Kanal im selben Fenster. viewer-directory meldet otherChannels=1, sharedViewers=1 und exclusiveViewers=0. viewer-segments meldet dagegen avgOtherChannels=0 und exclusiveViewersPct=100. Die gemeinsame UI bezeichnet denselben Zuschauer zugleich als vollständig geteilt und vollständig exklusiv.
findings.evidence: Directory zählt in 328 alle Kanäle minus eins und behandelt in 415-418 nur other_ch=0 als exklusiv. Segments schließt den Heimkanal bereits in 1102 aus, zählt in 1117 jedoch ch<=1 als exklusiv und zieht in 1120 erneut eins ab. Der bestehende Test in 1568-1629 verlangt ausdrücklich das widersprüchliche Segmentverhalten.
findings.expected_behavior: Die gleichnamigen Cross-Channel-Kennzahlen derselben Viewer-Seite benötigen eine konsistente Definition. Welche Berechnung geändert werden darf, ist wegen des ausdrücklich gegenteiligen Regressionstests nicht eindeutig belegt; deshalb Klasse C und keine automatische Fixfreigabe.
findings.countermeasures: Kein Guard gleicht die beiden Berechnungen ab. Der Regressionstest schützt gerade die Segmentdefinition mit einem anderen Kanal. Das Frontend kombiniert die Ergebnisse beider Endpunkte in Viewers.tsx:498-505 und 636, statt sie getrennt zu erläutern.

findings.claim: Analytics database queries have no application execution deadline and can exhaust the shared dashboard pool.
findings.failure_scenario: With no externally configured PostgreSQL statement timeout, an unfinished maintenance transaction holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on twitch_stream_sessions. Concurrent authorized follower-funnel requests acquire every dashboard pool connection and then wait indefinitely in fetch_one. Other dashboard requests subsequently fail to acquire connections. The configured five-second acquisition/connect deadline does not terminate already executing queries.
findings.evidence: At baseline 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, follower_funnel.rs:73-95 directly awaits the query without a deadline. The same pattern appears in loyalty_curve.rs:63, lurker_analysis.rs:99-104, retention_curve.rs:65-99 and viewer_timeline.rs:144-157,212,444-500. tb-dashboard/src/main.rs:400 supplies tb_db::connect to the router; tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:2233-2238 and1003 pass that pool to these handlers. tb-db/src/pool.rs:10-11 uses read_only=false, so the statement_timeout at49 is not applied. DbConfig only specifies acquisition/connect deadlines. The checked router layers impose no request timeout on these endpoints. ops/systemd/twitch-runtime-roles.sql:26-27 resets role settings and49-59 only sets search_path.
findings.expected_behavior: A stalled analytics query should eventually fail and release its shared connection. The repository demonstrates a bounded-query mechanism in connect_readonly, but does not specify the permitted duration of valid dashboard analytics queries. Therefore a new deadline policy remains C, not an automatic fix.
findings.countermeasures: Authentication, the plan gate and streamer ownership restrict callers but do not bound an authorized query. Pool maximum and acquisition timeout bound new acquisitions, not occupied connections. An externally configured database timeout could mitigate this scenario; actual production server/DSN settings were deliberately not inspected or probed. No tests or live requests were run.

findings.claim: Viewer timeline constructs JSON for every matching viewer before applying the response limit.
findings.failure_scenario: A large recorded session contains 20,000 matching viewers with 120 disjoint presence spans each. An authorized request with limit=1 still constructs approximately 2.4 million span JSON objects before discarding 19,999 viewer payloads. On a memory-constrained deployment that can hold the fetched spans and selected response but not these additional discarded payloads, this request causes allocation failure or an OOM kill instead of returning the single requested viewer.
findings.evidence: At baseline 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, viewer_timeline.rs:212 fetches all spans,223-238 retains them in a HashMap,332-370 constructs all matching viewer payloads including spans_json, and373-379 sorts and applies take(limit) only afterwards. The output limit is clamped at141. Presence producers retain all filtered chatters at tb-monitoring/src/chatters_poller.rs:409-413,430-488; the transport follows all chatter pages at tb-transport-twitch/src/chat.rs:789-832. The checked presence primary key only deduplicates identical session/viewer/timestamp triples, not total viewers or spans.
findings.expected_behavior: Preserve the documented filtering, ranking, total_unique_tracked and response limit while constructing span JSON only for selected viewers. docs/VIEWER_PRESENCE_TIMELINE.md:107,132-133 explicitly defines limit as a response limit, not a guarantee of bounded query work. This is therefore a C resource optimization with a concrete exhaustion scenario, not justification for silently capping legitimate history.
findings.countermeasures: The session ownership lookup, plan gate, excluded-login filter and 1..1000 response limit are present. They do not prevent intermediate JSON construction for discarded viewers. Database compression only reduces storage and does not bound Rust JSON allocations. No measured production memory threshold or reproduced OOM is claimed; this is static analysis of the allocation path.

findings.claim: Concurrent chat ingestion can give one viewer response conflicting message totals for the same window.
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated Plus partner requests their own viewer directory. An existing presence row has messages=0 when fetch_window_viewer_rows reads it. The bot commits a legitimate chat message before viewer_window_metadata runs. The response then contains totalMessages=0 and isLurker=true alongside windowPresenceMessages=1 and hasRawMessages=true. The detail handler has the same interleaving between its overview query and metadata query.
findings.evidence: At the fixed SHA, /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/viewers.rs:196-213 reads SUM(sc.messages); :292 and :322 execute the aggregate and metadata independently through PgPool. The metadata query at :112-127 reads the same session counters again. Both results are returned at :428-443. The twin is at :598-654 and :874-886. Concurrent ingestion is concrete: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-chat/src/chatter_tracking.rs:257-278 inserts the raw message, :358-373 increments messages, and :397 commits.
findings.expected_behavior: The two message-total fields describe the same viewer and time window and would agree in a consistent snapshot. No explicit request-level snapshot guarantee was found, so whether live analytical responses must provide that consistency remains a product decision; this is C, not an automatic-fix candidate.
findings.countermeasures: The plan gate and streamer-scope guard restrict access but do not serialize ingestion with reads. The writer transaction makes each ingestion atomic, and messages=messages+1 protects increments; neither protects multiple independent reader queries. Each individual SELECT is consistent, but the handler does not use a shared snapshot.

findings.claim: Repeated observations of one broadcast count as three sessions and unlock match scores.
findings.failure_scenario: A successful stream-list response temporarily omits an ongoing broadcast twice, with the same stream ID and started_at reappearing after each omission. The poller closes each current row and creates another row with the original started_at. After the final closure, the candidate has three overlapping rows starting at 18:00 and ending at 18:30, 19:30 and 20:30, but only one actual broadcast. Against a viewer with three genuine sessions, schedule() reports candidate.sessions=3 and match_score() returns a non-null score instead of treating the candidate as having insufficient history.
findings.evidence: At fixed SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, matching.rs:107 counts distinct (started_at, ended_at) pairs, whereas :79 merges the same overlapping rows into one interval. The inflated count satisfies the minimum-history gate at :172 and enables scores at :195. Reachability is established by /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-monitoring/src/poller/engine.rs:525-529,593-601, which finalizes an omitted stream and ensures a session when it reappears; /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-monitoring/src/sessions/tracker.rs:241-258 preserves the broadcast start time when inserting again. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/community.rs:110-120 loads all three completed rows without broadcast deduplication.
findings.expected_behavior: One broadcast must contribute one session to the minimum-three-sessions requirement. matching.rs:58 explicitly requires duplicate/overlapping observations not to boost a match, :106 requires counting distinct sessions rather than duplicate rows, and :194 requires at least three sessions per person for a score.
findings.countermeasures: Interval merging protects slot weights and observed-overlap minutes, and the BTreeSet removes exact endpoint duplicates. Neither protects session count when end times differ. SessionStore checks only currently open sessions at /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-monitoring/src/sessions/store.rs:247-271, so its start serialization does not prevent reopening an already closed broadcast. The session indexes at /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/migrations/20260601000000_baseline_schema.sql:2605-2607 are nonunique. The existing duplicate-history test covers identical endpoints only. No builds, tests, network requests or mutations were performed.

findings.claim: Die Werbeplan-API gibt bei wiedervergebenem Twitch-Login fremde Konto-Snapshots zurück.
findings.failure_scenario: Konto 111 hat gespeicherte Werbe-Snapshots mit twitch_login='recycled'. Nach Umbenennung und Wiedervergabe dieses Namens ist Konto 222 ein aktiver Partner mit Login 'recycled'. Dessen gültige Session darf GET /twitch/api/v2/ads-schedule aufrufen. Solange Konto 222 noch keine eigenen Snapshots hat, erscheinen die Daten von Konto 111 als current und history. Bei weniger als zehn eigenen Snapshots mischt history weiterhin fremde Daten hinein.
findings.evidence: Alle Quellen am festen SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af gelesen. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/ads_schedule.rs:61-70 filtert ausschließlich LOWER(twitch_login), ohne twitch_user_id oder zeitliche Grenze; Zeilen 83-105 geben die gefundenen Daten zurück. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/ads_schedule_collector.rs:97-115 und /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/ad_manager.rs:1502-1531 hängen Snapshots samt stabiler Benutzer-ID und damaligem Login an. Das Schema erlaubt diese historischen Zeilen unter unterschiedlichen IDs. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/auth/session.rs:1410-1437,1834-1860 authentifiziert den neuen Partner korrekt anhand seiner ID und liefert dessen aktuellen Login. Die Route ist in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:934-936 registriert.
findings.expected_behavior: Partner dürfen nur die Werbe-Snapshots ihrer authentifizierten Twitch-Benutzer-ID lesen. Namen sind keine Kontoberechtigung, ausdrücklich belegt in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/auth/session.rs:1410-1412. Die stabile ID ist bereits in Session und Snapshot vorhanden; eine Schemaänderung ist dafür nicht nötig.
findings.countermeasures: Der Scope-Resolver in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/auth/streamer_scope.rs:144-163 verhindert beliebige fremde Login-Parameter. Der Status-Gate in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/auth/partner_gate.rs:161-181 prüft den aktiven Partner. Beide schützen jedoch nicht vor historischen Snapshots einer anderen ID unter demselben Namen. SQL-Parameterbindung verhindert Injection, aber keine falsche Kontozuordnung. Der gezielt geprüfte Schwesterpfad des Werbemanagers verwendet die Session-ID und ID-gefilterte Historienabfragen. Keine Laufzeitprobes; externe, nicht versionierte Proxyregeln wurden nicht geprüft.

findings.claim: recent-bans meldet bei fehlgeschlagener Kanalzählung HTTP 200 mit channels_protected=0.
findings.failure_scenario: GET /twitch/api/v2/public/recent-bans bei vorhandenen aktiven Partnern: Die ersten beiden Abfragen auf twitch_ban_events gelingen, aber die anschließende Zählabfrage auf twitch_partners_all_state scheitert beispielsweise mit PoolTimedOut. findings.claim: Without database timeouts, stat-setting updates waiting on a locked plan row can exhaust the shared dashboard connection pool.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing streamer_plans row is held by an uncommitted transaction, and PostgreSQL has statement_timeout and lock_timeout disabled. Concurrent authenticated, CSRF-valid POST requests changing that streamer's command settings acquire every dashboard pool connection and then wait on the same row lock. With the default pool size this requires ten blocked updates. Other database-backed dashboard requests subsequently fail their five-second pool-acquisition deadline, while the blocked updates retain their connections until the lock is released.
findings.evidence: At revision 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, the anchored handler awaits INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE directly through the shared pool without an operation deadline. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/bin/tb-dashboard/src/main.rs:400 passes a pool created by tb_db::connect into the router. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-db/src/pool.rs:20-58 bounds connection acquisition but sets statement_timeout only for connect_readonly, not connect. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-config/src/lib.rs:125-135 establishes the ten-connection and five-second defaults. The inspected route and global middleware have no request deadline. Checked-in role provisioning resets role settings and does not establish query or lock deadlines. Twin unbounded write waits occur in the assigned scam-guard, silent, tip and sub-reminder settings handlers.
findings.expected_behavior: A blocked database operation should eventually release its pool connection and return a database error instead of indefinitely consuming shared dashboard capacity. The handler already supports database-error responses, but the permitted waiting budget is unspecified; selecting that policy requires a decision rather than an automatic B fix.
findings.countermeasures: Authentication, streamer scoping and CSRF restrict who can reach these writes. Pool capacity and acquisition timeouts bound connection counts and new waiters, but do not bound a statement after acquisition. A configured PostgreSQL statement_timeout or lock_timeout could prevent the scenario; live values were not inspected. The related reminder sender bounds its network call to eight seconds, so that ordinary send alone does not establish an indefinite lock. No security exploit or actual production outage is asserted.

findings.claim: Network-statistics requests can exhaust the shared database pool while waiting indefinitely for a table lock.

The configured default pool_max is 10 and acquisition timeout is 5 seconds.

These examples do not establish a mandatory deadline for the reviewed SQL routes, so this remains C rather than an automatic-fix B.
findings.countermeasures: Pool size and acquisition timeouts bound connection count and how long additional requests wait, but do not end queries already holding connections. Network profile enrichment has a timeout, single-flight guard, and negative cache; those guards run after its database read. External DSN, PostgreSQL, or proxy settings could impose additional limits and were not inspected under the read-only restrictions. findings.claim: A superseded network-profile refresh can overwrite a newer cache and clear its ownership marker.
findings.failure_scenario: Refresh A claims the slot at t=0 for a network containing Alice. Its Helix call succeeds within five seconds, but its worker is delayed before cache publication until after t=6. Bob becomes active in the meantime. Request B sees the expired marker, refreshes Alice and Bob, and publishes their profiles. A then resumes and replaces B's map with its Alice-only map, stamped as freshly cached. Bob's profile is consequently missing for up to an hour. If A resumes while B is still running, A also clears B's in-flight marker.
findings.evidence: Lines 180-190 reclaim an in-flight slot solely by elapsed time. Lines 197-218 then publish an entire replacement map and unconditionally clear in_flight without checking whether the publishing request still owns the slot. Production uses a multithreaded Tokio runtime in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/bin/tb-dashboard/src/main.rs:306-307. The cache TTL is 3600 seconds at line 117.
findings.expected_behavior: Once a replacement refresh owns the slot, a superseded refresh must not overwrite the replacement's data or release its ownership marker. The single-flight checks and stale-slot recovery test establish the intended refresh coordination.
findings.countermeasures: The mutex prevents simultaneous memory mutation. The five-second Helix timeout and one-second tolerance normally reduce overlap, but do not bound scheduling delay after a successful fetch. The stale-slot test at lines 755-788 supplies only an old timestamp, not an old task capable of subsequently publishing. This scheduling scenario was assessed statically, not reproduced.

findings.claim: Abandoned public raid onboarding requests accumulate OAuth records indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated unauthenticated GET /twitch/raid/auth requests with no parameters create distinct persistent states. If the requester never completes Twitch authorization, those rows remain after the 600-second validity period and across restarts. Continued requests grow the shared database and its indexes without reclamation, eventually exhausting finite storage.
findings.evidence: raid_pages.rs:154-176 explicitly permits public onboarding and calls the bridge. The internal handler accepts public:website_onboarding at raid_oauth.rs:375-376. Production wiring constructs StateStore at tb-bot/main.rs:913-928; raid_oauth_impl.rs:998-1002 generates a fresh state and persists it on every call. state_store.rs:105-124 inserts it, while lookup and consume only select valid states. Targeted fixed-SHA searches found cleanup_expired only in its declaration and its test, with no production caller. The broad expiry DELETE in migration 20260930220200_token_storage.sql:16 runs only during migration.
findings.expected_behavior: Expired abandoned raid states should be reclaimed without requiring a successful callback. StateStore::cleanup_expired explicitly implements that operation, and tests/state_store.rs:125-151 verifies removal while preserving other platforms.
findings.countermeasures: The 10-second bridge timeout bounds individual HTTP calls, not persistent record growth. Expiry checks prevent reuse but do not delete rows. Successful callbacks consume their states, but abandoned flows never reach that path. No external database cleanup schedule was verified; this is a native-runtime finding, not a demonstrated live denial-of-service attack.

findings.claim: Public recent-raid requests can hold every dashboard database connection indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario: With PostgreSQL statement_timeout and lock_timeout disabled, an uncommitted transaction holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on twitch_raid_history. Send as many concurrent public recent-raids requests as pool_max. Each request acquires a connection and waits indefinitely inside SELECT; unrelated dashboard queries then fail their pool-acquisition deadlines until the lock is released.
findings.evidence: raids.rs:40 awaits recent_raids without a deadline; the loader at tb-analytics/raids.rs:28-44 directly awaits fetch_all. The public route is registered at tb-dashboard-api/lib.rs:129-132. tb-dashboard/main.rs:400 uses tb_db::connect, whose pool.rs:10-23 selects read_only=false. pool.rs:44 bounds acquisition only; the 20-second statement_timeout at lines 47-52 is installed exclusively for read-only pools. The inspected router composition and server invocation add no request deadline. Assigned raid analytics and network analytics handlers use the same pool and have the same exposure.
findings.expected_behavior: A stalled external database operation should release its request and pool capacity within a finite operational deadline. The exact deadline and whether it belongs in PostgreSQL or application code require an operational decision, so this remains C.
findings.countermeasures: Pool size and acquisition timeouts bound active connections and later acquisition attempts, but not already executing queries. SQL row limits do not limit lock waits. An externally configured PostgreSQL timeout could defeat this scenario; live database, DSN options and proxy settings were not inspected under the read-only contract.

findings.claim: Follow attribution buffers the complete follow-by-raid cross product.
findings.failure_scenario: A selected session contains F follow events and R retention-linked incoming raids. The attribution query returns F times R rows because each follow joins every raid in that session. For example, 20,000 follows and 50 raids produce 1,000,000 rows for one session; repeating such sessions within the permitted window exhausts finite dashboard memory while materializing rows, even though the response contains only counts and per-source aggregates.
findings.evidence: raid_analytics.rs:568-589 joins follows to sessions and then joins twitch_raid_retention solely on target_session_id, without aggregation, DISTINCT or a row limit. Line 594 fetches the entire result into a Vec. Lines 603-618 only reduce that vector to counts and a source map. The requested window can span 3650 days at line 445, and table definitions do not cap events or raids per session.
findings.expected_behavior: Preserve full-window attribution semantics without materializing every follow/raid pair in application memory. Choosing equivalent SQL aggregation or bounded processing requires a structural change, so this remains C.
findings.countermeasures: The extended-plan gate and streamer scope restrict callers and channels. The 50-row incoming-raids limit and 50-entry retention-curve sample apply to separate queries and do not bound this result. A finite time window bounds dates, not join cardinality. No runtime memory measurement was performed.

findings.claim: Network raid analytics materializes the entire all-time manual raid history.
findings.failure_scenario: When accumulated manual_chat_command rows exceed what the dashboard process can materialize, one authorized network-analytics request exhausts memory: it fetches every matching historical row, constructs an additional JSON object for each, and serializes the entire list. The history can continue growing across years, so there is no dataset-size ceiling protecting the request.
findings.evidence: raid_network_analytics.rs:138-148 selects manual raids without a date filter, limit or pagination and uses fetch_all. Lines 149-164 create a second full-sized manual_list, included in the response at lines 185-193. The raid-history migration defines a growing hypertable and compression at 20260630130000_reconcile_event_hypertables.sql:160-170, not a result-size cap.
findings.expected_behavior: An admin listing should not require arbitrarily large in-memory results. However, this endpoint explicitly promises the all-time manual listing; selecting pagination, a window or another delivery contract changes behavior and therefore remains C.
findings.countermeasures: Admin-only authorization limits exposure but does not bound history size. Database compression reduces stored size, not the decoded row vector and JSON response. The separate raid-history loader clamps to 500 rows and public recent-raids clamps to 10; neither safeguard applies to this endpoint. No production dataset size or memory limit was probed.

findings.claim: Raid metric recalculation rejects the string raid IDs supplied by both HTTP handlers.
findings.failure_scenario: A raid has a target session and human chatters satisfying the retention windows. Both handlers serialize raid_id as a JSON string, so every input is discarded. raid-analytics returns zero retention, overlap and new-chatters metrics; raid-retention always uses stored metrics rather than recalculating them.
findings.evidence: At fixed SHA 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, line 48 uses as_i64(), which does not parse JSON strings. Lines 54-56 return immediately when the map is empty. The two production callers emit raid_id.to_string() at lines 303 and 487. Lines 527-530 substitute default zero metrics. The helper tests instead supply a numeric raid_id at line 969, hiding this caller/helper mismatch.
findings.expected_behavior: The helper must calculate metrics for the inputs actually constructed by both handlers. The recalculation comments, retention source reporting at lines 384-405, and positive helper assertions at lines 1012-1019 establish the intended behavior.
findings.countermeasures: Both routes are registered and guarded by the extended-plan and streamer-scope checks. These guards do not alter JSON value types. Stored fallback protects only raid-retention, not raid-analytics, and cannot provide its advertised recalculated bot filtering.

findings.claim: Joining every raid in a session duplicates follow events in raid analytics.
findings.failure_scenario: A target session receives raids at 10:00 and 11:00. One new viewer first chats at 11:05 and follows at 11:10, with no earlier rollup entry. The query produces two rows for this single follow, reports total_follows=2 and raid_follows=2, and credits both raid sources.
findings.evidence: Lines 581-582 join retention rows solely by target_session_id and then their matching history rows. Lines 604-612 count the resulting rows, and lines 613-617 increment each source. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/bot/migrations/twitch_analytics_schema.sql:816-834 has a primary key on (raid_id, executed_at), not target_session_id, so multiple raids in one session are valid.
findings.expected_behavior: One stored follow event must contribute once to total_follows and once to the raid/organic partition. Attribution to raid sources must not create additional follower events.
findings.countermeasures: Streamer ownership and followed_at session/window filters constrain which events are selected, not join cardinality. There is no DISTINCT, event-ID grouping, or single-raid selection before the Rust counters.

findings.claim: Raid analytics attributes follows that happened before the raid to that raid.
findings.failure_scenario: During a session starting at 09:00, a new viewer follows at 10:30, a raid arrives at 11:00, and the viewer first chats at 11:05. With no pre-session chatter history, the 10:30 follow is labeled raid and credited to the 11:00 raider.
findings.evidence: The CASE at lines 570-573 compares sc.first_message_at with rh.executed_at, but never compares fe.followed_at with the raid timestamp. The follow is selected because lines 576-578 only require it to fall inside the stream session. Lines 613-624 then expose the false raid attribution and conversion rate.
findings.expected_behavior: A follow predating a raid cannot be attributed to that later raid. The fields follow_source, raid_source and follows_attributed explicitly represent attribution of the follow event, not attribution of a later chat message.
findings.countermeasures: The historical-chatter exclusion at lines 583-586 does not establish follow chronology. Neither the session bounds nor the requested-window filter prevents a pre-raid follow within the same session.

findings.claim: Raid retention and source analytics count failed raid attempts as completed raids.
findings.failure_scenario: An attempted raid to a currently tracked live target fails because the source has no valid credential. A history row is recorded with success=false. The retention worker subsequently creates its rollup, and the dashboard displays this failed attempt with viewersSent and includes it in raid counts, although no viewers were sent.
findings.evidence: The retention query at lines 243-250 has no success check; its analytics twin at lines 451-458 joins history without filtering rh.success. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-raid/src/raid_executor.rs:135-142 records this failure, and /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-monitoring/src/raid_retention.rs:43-51 scans history without a success predicate before inserting the rollup at lines 147-166.
findings.expected_behavior: Retention and received/sent raid statistics must exclude attempts that never started. The existing successful-raid invariant is explicit in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/raids.rs:25-40 and in the assigned network analytics handler at lines 78 and 93.
findings.countermeasures: The worker requires a matching target session, but a failed attempt can still target a live tracked channel. The rollup foreign key ensures a matching history record, not success. The dashboard response omits success/error fields, so it does not distinguish these rows as failed attempts.

findings.claim: Raid balance reports received raids as sent raids.

The assigned network handler correctly separates source and target aggregates at lines 71-99.

findings.claim: An empty from parameter suppresses the nonempty from_broadcaster history filter.
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated admin requests /twitch/raid/history?from=&from_broadcaster=alpha while history contains raids from alpha and other streamers. The endpoint returns unfiltered history instead of only alpha's raids. Whitespace-only from has the same effect.

findings.expected_behavior: The first nonempty alias must win, as explicitly stated in the handler's line-42 contract. A nonempty from_broadcaster must remain effective when from is blank.
findings.countermeasures: The admin-only guard prevents public access but does not validate alias values. Loader normalization recognizes the blank value only after the alternative filter has already been discarded.

findings.claim: SQL-Fehler in Session-Details werden als erfolgreiche Nullzahlen und leere Listen ausgegeben.

Der vorhandene analytics_request_failed-Fehlerpfad der Hauptabfrage unterscheidet Datenbankausfälle bereits korrekt.

findings.claim: SQL-Fehler der Session-Ereignisabfragen erscheinen als erfolgreiche leere Ereignislisten.
findings.failure_scenario: Für eine berechtigt abrufbare Session liegen Raid-Ereignisse vor. Die Session-Metadaten werden erfolgreich gelesen, aber die Raid-Abfrage scheitert beim Erwerb einer Poolverbindung. Der Handler liefert HTTP 200 mit raids=[] statt den bestehenden Raids oder einer Fehlermeldung. Entsprechende Fehler bei Kanaländerungen und Follows verbergen diese Ereignisse ebenfalls.

Dieselben Fehlerverluste bestehen bei der Kanal-ID-Auflösung in Zeilen 385-392 sowie bei Kanaländerungen in Zeilen 397-409 und Follows in Zeilen 463-478. findings.claim: Rating-Lesefehler erscheinen im Stream-Report als nicht vorhandene Bewertung.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein angemeldeter Partner oder Twitch-Admin besitzt eine gespeicherte Bewertung samt Kommentar für den angeforderten Report. Die Report-Abfrage gelingt, die anschließende Rating-Abfrage scheitert etwa mit PoolTimedOut. Der Report wird trotzdem mit HTTP 200 und rating=null ausgeliefert. Die Bewertungsoberfläche zeigt keine bestehende Bewertung und setzt ihren Kommentarzustand auf einen leeren Text zurück.

Das if let Ok(Some(row)) in Zeilen 264-281 unterscheidet Err nicht von Ok(None); Zeilen 284-288 senden die unverändert erfolgreiche Report-Antwort. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/bot/dashboard_v2/src/pages/StreamReports.tsx:673-680 setzt Rating und Kommentar anhand dieser Antwort zurück. Der vorhandene Test in Zeilen 838-891 verlangt das eingebettete eigene Rating. Der verwandte Own-Vote-Lookup desselben Moduls behandelt Err in Zeilen 541-560 ausdrücklich als analytics_request_failed.

findings.countermeasures: Die Benutzeridentität wird korrekt durch owner_login bestimmt und die Abfrage durch session_id, Variante und rated_by eingeschränkt. Diese Schutzschichten verhindern keine Abfragefehler. Report-Lookup und A/B-Vote-Lookup propagieren Fehler bereits; nur das eingebettete Rating verliert sie. findings.claim: Fehlgeschlagene Bot-Auflösung lässt konfigurierte Bots in internen Stream-Bestenlisten erscheinen.
findings.failure_scenario: Ein eigener Bot ist ausschließlich über eine der unterstützten Bot-Nutzernummern konfiguriert, steht nicht in KNOWN_CHAT_BOTS und besitzt Chatter-Daten. Die dynamische Login-Auflösung scheitert vorübergehend, während Kanalauflösung und anschließende Kennzahlenabfragen erfolgreich sind. Die Ausschlussliste enthält diesen Bot dann nicht; seine Nachrichten beziehungsweise Anwesenheit werden als Zuschauerleistung mit HTTP 200 ausgegeben.
findings.evidence: Der Handler übernimmt in Zeile 98 die Ausschlussliste ohne Fehlerstatus und reicht sie in Zeile 100 an die Auswertung weiter. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/viewer_exclusion.rs:53-77 ersetzt Fehler der unterstützten Nutzernummern-Auflösung durch Vec::new; Zeilen 81-101 ergänzen anschließend nur bekannte Bots, direkt konfigurierte Logins und den Streamer. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/stream_kennzahlen.rs:278-281 verwendet diese Liste für die Session-Auswertungen. Der Primärhandler beschreibt in Zeilen 87-88 ausdrücklich Bestenlisten ohne Bots.
findings.expected_behavior: Die Antwort sollte bei gescheiterter erforderlicher Bot-Auflösung nicht uneingeschränkt als botbereinigte Auswertung gelten. Die gewünschte Fehlerstrategie für diese bewusst best-effort implementierte Zusatzauflösung ist jedoch nicht eindeutig belegt; deshalb C statt automatischer Fixfreigabe.
findings.countermeasures: Bekannte Bots und zusätzlich konfigurierte Bot-Logins bleiben auch bei diesem Fehler ausgeschlossen. Der Befund betrifft nur eigene Bots, deren Login ausschließlich aus der Nutzernummer aufgelöst werden muss. Normale Kennzahlenfehler werden bereits als 503 propagiert; die vorgelagerte Auflösung entzieht ihren Fehler diesem Pfad. Der Helfer protokolliert ihn auf Debug-Niveau. Entscheidung über 503 oder belastbaren Ersatz bleibt offen.

findings.claim: Concurrent partner removal can zero existing historical raid counts in a cached streamer comparison.
findings.failure_scenario: On a cache miss, partner A has stream sessions and five confirmed historical raids in the requested period. The session query takes its snapshot while A is active. An overlapping admin clear/failed request changes A's status to departnered before the raid query takes its snapshot. The session result still includes A, but the independently filtered raid result excludes A. The response retains A with confirmedRaids=0, omits A's raids from network totals, and caches that combination for 60 seconds. Neither the pre-removal nor post-removal database state has that combination.
findings.evidence: At fixed commit 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, load_session_metrics independently selects active partners at lines 311-339 and fetches through PgPool at 362-363. load_raid_metrics independently selects active partners at 391-402 and fetches through PgPool at 490-491. Lines 721-725 run these separate statements with tokio::join!, without a shared transaction snapshot. Line 560 substitutes RaidMetric::default() for missing raid results; lines 613-630 aggregate only matching session-cohort logins; lines 752-756 cache the response. The reachable admin verify handler calls departner_streamer for clear/failed at admin_streamers.rs:525-529. streamers_crud.rs:495-523 updates twitch_partners.status; its remaining follow-ups at 525-555 do not delete historical sessions or raids. storage_pg_v2_partner_archive_split.sql:117-118 excludes non-active status from the partner view.
findings.expected_behavior: For a coherent active-partner cohort, A should either be omitted after removal or retain the historical raid metrics corresponding to the cohort snapshot that included A. The response describes an active-partner cohort and confirmed raid measurements at lines 647-649. However, no explicit cross-query snapshot-consistency contract was found, and stale public responses are intentionally permitted. Therefore this remains C pending a consistency-policy decision, not an automatic fix.
findings.countermeasures: The per-period mutex at lines 690-704 prevents concurrent cache builders for the same period, and each SQL statement has its own coherent snapshot. The 60-second cache policy explicitly allows stale data. Neither protection coordinates the two SQL snapshots with partner lifecycle mutations. The active-partner unique indexes at storage_pg_v2_partner_archive_split.sql:120-126 prevent duplicate active identities, not this mixed-cohort result. The raid-only cohort filter at lines 620-623 protects the opposite interleaving but does not repair a missing raid result for an already selected session row.

findings.claim: Whitespace-equivalent plan keys can hide a configured Stripe price during resolution.
findings.failure_scenario: With configured Stripe support and STRIPE_PRICE_ID_MAP containing {" plus ":{"12":"price_plus_12m"},"plus":{"1":"price_plus_1m"}}, parsing produces two entries named plus. Resolving plus for cycle 1 examines only the first entry and returns None. The catalog disables monthly checkout, and checkout redirects with missing_stripe_price_id despite the valid monthly slot.
findings.evidence: Fixed-source /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/billing/catalog.rs:475 trims plan keys, but lines 493-495 append without consolidating equivalent keys. Lines 542-546 select the first plan before searching its cycles. Caller context in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing_page.rs:220-223 and 699-706 propagates the missing resolution into checkout failure and unavailability.
findings.expected_behavior: The parser documents a normalized map and accepts both nonempty IDs and cycles 1/12. Equivalent normalized keys should have a defined collision policy rather than silently hiding an accepted slot. Whether to merge, replace, or reject duplicate normalized plans is not specified, so this remains C rather than an automatic fix.
findings.countermeasures: Canonical configuration with one entry per normalized plan avoids the issue. PRICE_ID_DEFAULTS is empty at the fixed source, so no default rescues resolution. Checkout reports the missing price and does not send an invalid Stripe request; this is configuration loss, not a demonstrated security bypass.

findings.claim: The monthly billing catalog describes a calendar-month subscription as a fixed 30-day cycle.
findings.failure_scenario: For Plus with cycle_months=1, catalog_json returns cycle_label="30 Tage". A paid calendar-month period from February 1 to March 1, 2027 lasts 28 days, so the returned duration does not match the subscription interval.

findings.claim: Billing lookup failures can grant a trial to a paying subscriber and suppress their paid plan for 30 days.
findings.failure_scenario: A user has an active pro subscription, trial_ever_granted=0, no manual override and first_login_at older than 24 hours. The subscription SELECT encounters a transient database error, such as query cancellation, but subsequent queries succeed. The helper returns false, auto-grant commits an analytics_trial override and consumes the once-only flag. Plan resolution then returns the trial instead of pro, removing paid entitlements until the override expires. Self-claim can similarly return HTTP 200/granted despite the failed eligibility check.
findings.evidence: Fixed source 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. trial.rs:247-250 maps every unsuccessful billing lookup to false. Both grant paths use this value before opening their write transaction (142-146, 282-285), then commit the trial override (181-215, 321-350). Context /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/plan.rs:384-389 invokes auto-grant before resolution; 480-491 returns an active manual override before consulting billing. Its lines 71-97 show pro includes social.auto_post and raid.priority whereas analytics_trial does not. Context /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing.rs:38-44 maps Granted to HTTP 200. Static inspection only.
findings.expected_behavior: An active paid subscription must prevent trial granting and remain effective, as explicitly asserted by trial.rs:435-457 and 594-634. An unexpected database failure must not be treated as evidence that no subscription exists or produce a successful grant; TrialOutcome::Error is documented for database errors at lines 66-67 and mapped to HTTP 500 by the handler.
findings.countermeasures: Existing once-only and manual-right checks do not protect a first-time subscriber without a manual override. Because the failed billing SELECT occurs outside the later transaction, it does not prevent that transaction from committing. The handler verifies partner identity but has no separate paid-subscription guard. Comments intentionally tolerate a missing legacy table, but the wildcard also swallows unrelated operational errors. Existing paid-subscription tests cover successful reads, not read failures.

findings.claim: Blocked trial UPSERTs can exhaust the shared database pool.
findings.failure_scenario: With PostgreSQL statement_timeout and lock_timeout disabled, another transaction updates an eligible streamer's streamer_plans row and remains open. Authenticated trial-start requests read the previous committed eligibility state, then block on ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. Each blocked request retains its checked-out connection. Once concurrent requests occupy pool_max connections, other dashboard operations cannot acquire connections and fail, while the trial requests never produce an outcome until the blocking transaction ends.
findings.evidence: Pinned source 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/trial.rs:146-211 holds a transaction through the awaited UPSERT without a deadline; the auto-grant repeats this at 285-348. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing.rs:20-44 directly awaits the grant for authenticated partners. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/bin/tb-dashboard/src/main.rs:400-403 constructs the ordinary writable pool, and 476-482 shares it with the router. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-db/src/pool.rs:41-57 bounds connection acquisition but installs statement_timeout only for read_only connections.
findings.expected_behavior: Recommend a finite database-operation deadline and cancellation cleanup so a blocked grant releases its connection and reaches the existing error outcome. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/trial.rs:127-133 provides TrialOutcome::Error, mapped to HTTP 500 by /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing.rs:39-44. No required timeout duration or bounded-completion contract is established, so this remains C.
findings.countermeasures: Pool size and acquisition timeout bound connection count and acquisition waits, not execution after checkout. LIMIT 1 bounds returned rows, not lock waits. Paid-plan and already-used guards exclude ineligible users but not the described eligible user. The 20-second statement timeout is conditional on the readonly pool constructor, which the inspected dashboard startup does not use. External PostgreSQL or proxy deadlines could mitigate the scenario; their live configuration was not inspected, and no claim of an observed production outage is made.

findings.claim: Plan resolution can replace paid subscription entitlements with a trial after the paid-subscription lookup fails.

The error handler at /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/trial.rs:268-273 cannot catch this error because the subscription helper already converted it to false. findings.claim: Without PostgreSQL query deadlines, blocked plan resolution can exhaust the dashboard's shared connection pool.
findings.failure_scenario: With statement_timeout and lock_timeout disabled, a maintenance transaction holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on twitch_billing_subscriptions indefinitely blocks authenticated billing-catalog requests. Plan resolution first awaits the trial eligibility check, whose paid-subscription SELECT waits on that lock. Enough simultaneous requests occupy every shared pool connection; other database-backed requests then time out acquiring connections. The original requests never reach their fallback while the lock persists.
findings.evidence: Verified against 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. Primary plan.rs:388-389 awaits trial eligibility without a deadline. Context /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/trial.rs:233-245,263-283 performs and awaits the subscription query before other eligibility guards. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing_page.rs:643-678 reaches this path for an authenticated partner. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/bin/tb-dashboard/src/main.rs:400,476-483 wires the ordinary shared pool. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-db/src/pool.rs:20-57 sets an acquisition deadline, but sets statement_timeout only in read-only mode. Inspected outer router layers in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:2204-2314 contain no request deadline.
findings.expected_behavior: The billing catalog explicitly falls back to the free-plan snapshot on database errors at billing_page.rs:666-678. Database lock contention should have a finite failure boundary so requests can terminate and connections become available again. The sources do not specify the allowed query duration or cancellation policy, so selecting that policy remains C rather than an automatic B fix.
findings.countermeasures: Pool size and acquire_timeout bound connection acquisition, not a query already holding a connection. Authentication restricts the catalog to signed-in callers. connect_readonly supplies a 20-second statement timeout, but the inspected dashboard entry point uses connect instead. Effective production PostgreSQL and DSN timeout settings were not inspected under the read-only contract; an externally configured statement or lock timeout would bound this scenario. Recommendation only: establish a bounded database execution/cancellation policy for the ordinary pool.

findings.claim: A stale billing check can install a trial over an already active paid subscription.
findings.failure_scenario: An eligible account has no active subscription or manual override. A trial request reads paid_billing=false. A valid Stripe webhook then commits an active pro subscription and completes its ordinary, zero-bonus plan sync. The trial request subsequently begins its transaction, finds no blocking manual override, and installs analytics_trial. Plan resolution now selects that trial rather than the paid pro subscription, removing paid entitlements such as social.auto_post for the trial's duration. The automatic grant caches the same stale result at line 283.
findings.evidence: trial.rs:144 and :283 query subscriptions before beginning the grant transaction, then use that cached Boolean at :183/:321 without another billing read. Subscription writes and commits are reachable in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing_webhook.rs:215-259 and /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/stripe/webhook_apply.rs:423-460,705-733. Its ordinary sync at :506-544 updates plan_name/expires_at but leaves manual trial fields alone. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/plan.rs:480-492 makes an active manual override terminal; :71-97 shows pro has social.auto_post and analytics_trial does not. Context was read from the fixed SHA.
findings.expected_behavior: trial.rs:98-100 promises not to override an existing paid plan. Tests at :435-458 and :594-633 require active paid subscriptions to block grants; the latter explicitly documents the loss of paid social.auto_post as the incorrect behavior being prevented.
findings.countermeasures: The paid-subscription query recognizes both login and user ID and active/trialing plans, but its result becomes stale before any grant transaction starts. Even serializable isolation of that later transaction would not cover the earlier billing read. Webhook deduplication coordinates event retries, not trial eligibility. The postcommit subscription sync does not clear the manual trial, so it does not repair the resulting paid-plan suppression.

findings.claim: Concurrent trial requests can both grant and reset the one-time trial expiry.
findings.failure_scenario: With a writable pool under READ COMMITTED, two eligible requests for the same account both read trial_ever_granted=0 and an empty/free manual plan before either writes. Each executes its unconditional UPSERT and commits. Both self-claims return Granted, or both automatic checks return true, and the later write replaces the first trial's expiry and grant notes rather than treating the trial as already used.
findings.evidence: trial.rs:149-181 and :288-323 perform unlocked checks; :197-202 and :334-339 have no WHERE condition on trial_ever_granted. Each operation independently computes now+30 days at :189-191/:325-328. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing.rs:38-44 exposes Granted as HTTP 200. Automatic checks are reached from /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/plan.rs:384-390. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-db/src/pool.rs:40-58 permits multiple connections and sets no stronger isolation. Context was read at the fixed SHA; no tests were run.
findings.expected_behavior: trial.rs:1-10 defines exactly one trial per streamer, :98-100 explicitly promises idempotency, and :62-63 defines AlreadyUsed for an existing grant. The existing test at :419-432 requires the second automatic grant to return false rather than renew the trial.
findings.countermeasures: The account primary key serializes conflicting UPSERT writes and prevents duplicate rows, but does not revalidate the earlier eligibility decision. Setting trial_ever_granted=1 in both writes is not an atomic claim. Authentication, partner-status and CSRF middleware in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/lib.rs:1003-1015 do not serialize eligible requests. findings.claim: Subscription deletion without metadata.customer_reference leaves paid raid priority enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: A Plus checkout creates a subscription whose own metadata lacks customer_reference. Checkout processing uses the session reference as fallback and writes plan_name=plus for the purchaser. A subsequent customer.subscription.deleted event has status=canceled and empty subscription metadata. The raw subscription becomes canceled, but the plan-sync payload has an empty reference, so synchronization silently does nothing. With no manual override or explicit boost switch, subsequent raid-score calculations still grant the canceled purchaser the Plus boost.
findings.evidence: Static source at 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. In the finding file, checkout supplies the reference fallback at 279-286; subscription lifecycle sync instead extracts the event alone at 311-314. The raw UPSERT preserves an existing reference at 369, but sync returns without writing when its reference is empty at 495-498, and affected_login_for_billing_refresh likewise returns None at 622-624 and 645-647. Context: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing_page.rs:232-265 puts customer_reference in session metadata, not subscription_data.metadata. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-raid/src/partner_score_refresh.rs:630-651 reads the unchanged streamer_plans row; /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/plan.rs:149-159 grants boost from plan_name=plus.
findings.expected_behavior: Deletion must remove the billing-derived paid plan and its raid priority. The finding file documents effective-plan mirroring at 9-12 and 481-488; its subscription_deleted_clears_plan_to_free test at 1110-1162 explicitly asserts this outcome. Omitting metadata must not defeat the customer association already retained in the subscription row.
findings.countermeasures: The raw UPSERT correctly preserves the customer association, and the raw plan resolver excludes canceled subscriptions. These protect other subscription-based entitlements but do not repair the raid mirror. Signature verification and event-ID deduplication do not supply the missing reference. Periodic raid refresh reads the stale mirror rather than the canceled subscription.

findings.claim: Invoice payment events can restore paid entitlements to an already canceled subscription.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing Plus subscription has status=canceled after its lifecycle deletion was processed. A later invoice.payment_succeeded event for an outstanding invoice on that same subscription is processed. The invoice branch changes status to active while retaining the canceled subscription's customer_reference and plan_id. The plan resolver consequently grants Plus entitlements again although the subscription remains canceled. The invoice.payment_failed branch produces the same result through past_due, which the resolver also accepts.
findings.evidence: At fixed commit 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af, the finding file constructs unconditional status=active at 736-748 and status=past_due at 759-771. upsert_subscription_state retains the customer reference and plan at 368-384, accepts the new status at 370-383, and overwrites persisted status at 432. Context: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-analytics/src/plan.rs:342 and 535-596 accepts active, trialing and past_due and returns their paid plan without excluding retained canceled_at or ended_at. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing_webhook.rs:226-235 forwards fresh invoice events directly to apply_event.
findings.expected_behavior: Collecting or failing to collect an invoice must not reactivate an ended subscription. Subscription lifecycle is explicitly the paid-state authority in the finding file at 9-12, and deletion is expected to clear paid status at 1110-1162. Invoice handling may recover an overdue live subscription, but must preserve an already terminal lifecycle state.
findings.countermeasures: The handler verifies signatures and atomically deduplicates events, but a legitimate fresh invoice event passes both checks. Existing-row status is loaded but never used to prevent terminal-state replacement. Retaining canceled_at and ended_at does not help because the entitlement resolver selects by status.

findings.claim: A delayed older subscription snapshot can overwrite cancellation and restore a paid plan.
findings.failure_scenario: Two distinct events concern the same Plus subscription: an earlier customer.subscription.updated snapshot says active, and a later customer.subscription.deleted snapshot says canceled. The deletion is delivered first and clears the subscription and plan. The older update is then delivered or resent with a valid current delivery signature. Processing it rewrites the raw state to active and mirrors Plus again, restoring paid access despite the actual canceled subscription.
findings.evidence: Static source at 0ecae1370f1a80d1a101249b5c932663d69be8af. The finding file applies every subscription snapshot at 717-721, unconditionally overwrites status and plan at 429-442, and generates updated_at from processing time at 421. Its sync helper uses that same snapshot at 311-314. Context: /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing_webhook.rs:148-170 extracts no event-created timestamp; process_event at 215-258 deduplicates only the event ID and applies each fresh snapshot. Current subscription retrieval is restricted to checkout events at 374-399. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/migrations/20260601000000_baseline_schema.sql:462-477 and 1931-1935 contains no chronological state guard.
findings.expected_behavior: The stored effective plan must reflect the current subscription lifecycle, not whichever historical snapshot arrives last. The finding file identifies Stripe lifecycle as the paid-state authority at 9-12 and explicitly expects canceled subscriptions to become free at 1110-1162. A delayed pre-cancellation snapshot must not reverse that outcome.
findings.countermeasures: Signature verification authenticates delivery, not chronological freshness of the enclosed snapshot. Event-ID deduplication at 783-810 blocks identical replays only; the older update and newer deletion have different IDs. Transactions and the subscription primary key prevent duplicate rows but do not prevent stale state replacement.

findings.claim: Dünne Rechnungs-Events verlieren parallel aktualisierte Abo-Daten.
findings.failure_scenario: Der Bestand enthält plan_id=plus. Transaktion A aktualisiert dasselbe Abo durch customer.subscription.updated auf pro und hält noch dessen Zeilensperre. Transaktion B verarbeitet parallel invoice.payment_succeeded: Ihr ungesperrter SELECT sieht weiterhin plus und berechnet daraus die fehlenden Rechnungsfelder. Ihr UPSERT wartet auf A. Nachdem A committet, schreibt B die zuvor berechneten EXCLUDED-Werte zurück und setzt plan_id wieder auf plus. Entsprechend können neue Periodendaten, Menge oder Kundenreferenz verloren gehen. Die aktive Planauflösung liefert danach den alten Plan.

findings.countermeasures: Der Subscription-Primärschlüssel verhindert doppelte Zeilen, aber keinen Verlust durch vorab berechnete EXCLUDED-Werte. Event-Dedup serialisiert unterschiedliche Event-IDs nicht. Die konfliktzeitliche COALESCE-Prüfung in :438 schützt cancel_at_period_end tatsächlich; plan_id und die übrigen zusammengeführten Felder besitzen diesen Schutz nicht.

findings.claim: Large positive Stripe bonus_months metadata panics during webhook processing.

The value passes extraction and the positive-value guard. Duration::days receives 124000000000 days and panics because that exceeds Chrono's representable duration. This happens after the event and subscription state have committed; a subsequent delivery is classified as a duplicate and skips the plan/bonus sync.

The pinned dependency is Chrono 0.4.45 in /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/Cargo.lock:509-510. /home/nathanael/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/chrono-0.4.45/src/time_delta.rs:137-151 implements days using a panicking expect; lines 223-225 document its seconds bound. /home/nathanael/.worktrees/tb-vollreview-artefakte/rust/crates/tb-dashboard-api/src/handlers/billing_webhook.rs:240-248 commits core processing before invoking the affected sync.
